## [1631] Small fibre neuropathy: skin biopsy quantification, autonomic function testing

**Cluster**: small fibre neuropathy skin biopsy quantification autonomic function testing | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Small fiber neuropathy (SFN) selectively affects unmyelinated C-fibers and thinly myelinated A-delta nerve fibers responsible for thermal sensation, nociception, and autonomic function. Because conventional nerve conduction studies are normal, diagnosis relies on skin biopsy quantification of intraepidermal nerve fiber density and specialized autonomic testing.

### Core Teaching Points
- Small fiber neuropathy presents clinically with burning neuropathic pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia, paresthesias, and dysautonomia (orthostatic intolerance, gastroparesis, secretomotor changes, bowel/bladder dysfunction); large fiber modalities (vibration sense, proprioception, deep tendon reflexes, and muscle strength) are completely preserved. (PMID 41114676)
- Routine electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS) assess only large myelinated A-alpha and A-beta sensory and motor fibers, and are therefore entirely normal in isolated small fiber neuropathy, frequently leading to misdiagnosis. (PMID 42328949)
- Punch skin biopsy (typically 3-mm punch taken 10 cm above the lateral malleolus) with immunohistochemical staining for Protein Gene Product 9.5 (PGP 9.5) is the diagnostic gold standard, objectively demonstrating reduced Intraepidermal Nerve Fiber Density (IENFD) below the 5th percentile of age- and sex-adjusted normative values. (PMID 39179381)
- Autonomic function testing provides objective confirmation of small fiber involvement: Quantitative Sudomotor Axon Reflex Testing (QSART), thermoregulatory sweat testing (TST), and heart rate variability with deep breathing assess autonomic post-ganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic small fiber function. (PMID 40620177)
- Common identifiable secondary etiologies include impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes (most common), systemic autoimmune conditions (Sjogren syndrome, sarcoidosis, lupus), monoclonal gammopathies, celiac disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency), and amyloidosis. (PMID 41114676)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Role of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy in autoimmune-mediated or immune-complex small fiber neuropathy.
- Diagnostic accuracy of corneal confocal microscopy (measuring corneal sub-basal nerve plexus density) as a non-invasive surrogate for skin biopsy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Gold-standard diagnostic test for SFN: skin biopsy with PGP 9.5 quantification showing reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).
- Why nerve conduction studies are normal in SFN: NCS measures only large myelinated A-beta fibers; unmyelinated C and thinly myelinated A-delta fibers cannot be evaluated by routine NCS.
- Underlying metabolic cause: impaired glucose tolerance and early prediabetes are the most common identifiable triggers of painful small fiber neuropathy.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old woman with normal fasting glucose but impaired glucose tolerance on OGTT presenting with 12 months of severe burning feet pain and allodynia with normal EMG/NCS.
- A 40-year-old man with Sjogren syndrome presenting with orthostatic dizziness, dry skin, and distal paresthesias whose distal leg skin biopsy confirms reduced IENFD at 1.8 fibers/mm.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1632] Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy

**Cluster**: smoking cessation pharmacotherapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Tobacco use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition driven by physical nicotine addiction and behavioral conditioning. Combining first-line evidence-based pharmacotherapy—specifically varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy (NRT)—with behavioral counseling triples long-term smoking cessation rates.

### Core Teaching Points
- Combining evidence-based pharmacotherapy with structured behavioral counseling (cognitive behavioral strategies, motivational interviewing) is significantly more effective than either modality alone, achieving long-term quit rates 2 to 3 times higher than unassisted quit attempts. (PMID 39264407)
- First-line pharmacological options comprise: varenicline (nicotine acetylcholine receptor partial agonist), combination nicotine replacement therapy (NRT: long-acting transdermal patch plus a rapid-acting oral formulation such as gum, lozenge, inhalator, or spray), and bupropion sustained-release (atypical antidepressant and dopamine/norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor). (PMID 38137639)
- In high-quality network meta-analyses and randomized trials (e.g., EAGLES trial), varenicline and combination NRT demonstrate equivalent superior efficacy, both achieving significantly higher 6-month abstinence rates (approx. 25–30%) compared with bupropion monotherapy (15–20%) or single-agent NRT. (PMID 35233133)
- Varenicline binds with high affinity to alpha-4-beta-2 neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors as a partial agonist: stimulating moderate dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward system to alleviate nicotine craving and withdrawal symptoms, while competitively blocking nicotine from binding to blunt the rewarding effects of smoking. (PMID 42706202)
- The landmark EAGLES randomized trial (over 8,000 smokers with and without psychiatric disorders) firmly refuted historical neuropsychiatric warnings, demonstrating that varenicline and bupropion do NOT increase the incidence of serious neuropsychiatric adverse events (depression, suicidal ideation) compared with placebo or NRT. (PMID 41529951)
- Contraindications and safety pearls: bupropion is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of seizure disorder, eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia), or abrupt alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal due to a lowered seizure threshold; varenicline common side effects include nausea (minimized by taking with food and water) and vivid dreams. (PMID 39264407)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Long-term cardiovascular and pulmonary safety profiles of electronic nicotine delivery systems (e-cigarettes/vaping) utilized as smoking cessation tools.
- Optimal treatment duration of maintenance varenicline (extended 24 weeks vs standard 12 weeks) in heavy relapsing smokers.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- EAGLES trial landmark finding: varenicline does not increase serious neuropsychiatric adverse events or suicidality in smokers with or without psychiatric history.
- Most effective pharmacotherapy options: varenicline monotherapy and combination NRT (patch + rapid-acting oral NRT) are equally superior to single-agent NRT or bupropion.
- Bupropion contraindication: seizure disorder, active eating disorders, and abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives due to heightened seizure risk.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 45-year-old heavy smoker (20 cigarettes/day for 25 years) with stable depression on sertraline seeking the most effective pharmacotherapy to quit smoking permanently.
- A 38-year-old man with a history of idiopathic generalized epilepsy inquiring whether bupropion is safe to use for tobacco cessation.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1633] Smouldering Multiple Myeloma

**Cluster**: smouldering multiple myeloma | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Smouldering multiple myeloma (SMM) is an asymptomatic clonal plasma cell proliferative disorder positioned between MGUS and active multiple myeloma. Diagnosing SMM requires confirming bone marrow plasmacytosis >=10% or high serum M-protein in the absence of myeloma-defining events (CRAB criteria and SLiM biomarkers), with risk stratification identifying high-risk individuals who benefit from early therapeutic intervention.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnostic criteria for SMM require serum monoclonal protein (IgG or IgA) >=30 g/L (>=3.0 g/dL) or urinary monoclonal protein >=500 mg/24h, and/or clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10% to 59%, in the strict absence of end-organ damage (CRAB: Hypercalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions) or amyloidosis. (PMID 42533204)
- The International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) established 'SLiM' biomarkers of malignancy—Sixty percent bone marrow plasmacytosis (>=60%), Light chain ratio (involved/uninvolved serum free light chain ratio >=100), and MRI focal lesions (>1 focal lesion >=5 mm)—which define active, treatment-requiring myeloma regardless of CRAB symptoms due to an ~80% risk of progression within 2 years. (PMID 41571958)
- The updated IMWG '20/2/20' risk stratification model identifies high-risk SMM based on three risk factors: bone marrow plasma cells >20%, serum M-protein >2 g/dL, and involved-to-uninvolved free light chain ratio >20; patients with >=2 risk factors have a ~50% risk of progression to active myeloma at 2 years. (PMID 41565487)
- In patients with high-risk SMM, landmark randomized clinical trials (QuiRedex trial and ECOG E3A06 trial) established that early intervention with lenalidomide (alone or with dexamethasone) significantly delays progression to symptomatic myeloma and extends overall survival compared with observation alone. (PMID 35114153)
- Low- and intermediate-risk SMM patients should be managed with close active surveillance (clinical, biochemical, and whole-body low-dose CT or whole-body MRI every 3 to 6 months) without upfront cytotoxic or immunomodulatory therapy. (PMID 41604291)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Curative potential and long-term immunological impact of intensive quadruplet chemoimmunotherapy (daratumumab-KRd) followed by ASCT in high-risk SMM.
- Utility of circulating tumor plasma cells (CTCs) and liquid biopsy NGS panels in refining early progression prediction models.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- SLiM criteria defining active myeloma (not SMM): bone marrow plasma cells >=60%, involved:uninvolved FLC ratio >=100, or >1 focal marrow lesion on MRI.
- IMWG '20/2/20' high-risk SMM score: marrow plasma cells >20%, M-protein >2 g/dL, and FLC ratio >20 predict ~50% 2-year progression risk.
- Evidence for early intervention in high-risk SMM: lenalidomide-based therapy prolongs progression-free and overall survival over watchful waiting.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 58-year-old asymptomatic executive found to have an IgG kappa paraprotein of 34 g/L, bone marrow biopsy showing 25% clonal plasma cells, normal calcium, normal renal function, and normal skeletal MRI.
- A 64-year-old woman with known SMM whose involved-to-uninvolved serum free light chain ratio rises from 45 to 115, evaluated for classification as active multiple myeloma.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1634] soft tissue injuries

**Cluster**: soft tissue injuries | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Soft tissue injuries—comprising muscle strains, ligamentous sprains, tendon injuries, and contusions—represent the most frequent musculoskeletal presentations in sports medicine and emergency practice. Management paradigms have transitioned from the acute vasoconstrictive 'RICE' protocol to the comprehensive 'PEACE & LOVE' framework (Protect, Elevate, Avoid anti-inflammatory modalities, Compress, Educate & Load, Optimism, Vascularisation, Exercise). Accurate grading (Grade I: microscopic tear; Grade II: partial tear; Grade III: complete rupture), exclusion of fracture via validated rules (e.g., Ottawa Ankle Rules), and progressive functional rehabilitation determine safe return to play.

### Core Teaching Points
- The modern management of acute soft tissue injuries utilizes the PEACE & LOVE framework, which specifically discourages early routine NSAID and ice use because inhibiting acute inflammatory signaling impairs long-term tissue regeneration and tendon/ligament healing. (PMID 42087756)
- The Ottawa Ankle Rules reliably exclude fracture in acute ankle trauma (bone tenderness at posterior edge/tip of lateral or medial malleolus, or inability to bear weight both immediately and in the ED), reducing unneeded radiography with >98% sensitivity. (PMID 42093763)
- Early progressive active mobilization and mechanical loading ('Load' in PEACE & LOVE) stimulates collagen realignment, increases tensile strength, and accelerates return-to-sport compared to prolonged joint immobilization. (PMID 41716305)
- Complete structural tendon ruptures (e.g., Achilles tendon rupture, distal biceps tendon) require urgent assessment using clinical tests (Thompson/Simmonds squeeze test for Achilles) to decide between surgical repair versus functional bracing protocols. (PMID 41106927)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections in accelerating healing of acute Grade II muscle strains and partial tendon tears.
- Surgical repair versus non-operative functional rehabilitation with early weight-bearing in acute complete Achilles tendon ruptures.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Applying Ottawa Ankle and Foot Rules to eliminate unnecessary radiographs in acute ankle sprains.
- Physiological rationale for avoiding high-dose NSAIDs during the acute 48-72 hour phase of muscle and ligament healing.
- Diagnostic accuracy of the Thompson squeeze test in acute Achilles tendon rupture and recognizing false negatives from plantaris preservation.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 22-year-old soccer player sustains an acute inversion ankle sprain; he is able to walk 4 steps in the clinic, and has no bone tenderness over the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, navicular, or fifth metatarsal.
- A 40-year-old recreational runner feels a sudden 'pop' in his calf during a sprint; calf squeeze fails to elicit passive plantarflexion of the foot (positive Thompson test).

## [1635] Soft Tissue Sarcomas

**Cluster**: soft tissue sarcomas | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare, heterogeneous mesenchymal malignancies arising predominantly in extremity and trunk soft tissues. Core needle biopsy, high-resolution MRI, and limb-sparing wide local excision with adjuvant radiotherapy by a specialized multidisciplinary sarcoma team constitute the standard of care.

### Core Teaching Points
- Any soft tissue mass that is deep to the deep fascia, painful, enlarging, or greater than 5 cm in diameter ('golf ball size') must be considered malignant until proven otherwise; initial imaging is contrast-enhanced MRI of the affected compartment. (PMID 42000589)
- Percutaneous image-guided core needle biopsy along the longitudinal axis of the anticipated surgical incision is mandatory before any surgical manipulation; excisional biopsy ('whoops surgery') of an unstaged sarcoma violates anatomical tissue planes, dramatically increases local recurrence, and often requires extensive re-resection. (PMID 42500831)
- Histological grading (using the FNCLCC three-tier system based on tumor differentiation, mitotic count, and tumor necrosis) is the single most important histological predictor of distant metastatic recurrence and overall survival. (PMID 42505406)
- Limb-sparing surgery with wide local excision (aiming for microscopically clear 1-cm soft tissue or fascial margins) combined with preoperative or postoperative external beam radiotherapy provides local control rates exceeding 85–90% with survival equivalent to radical amputation. (PMID 42686333)
- First-line systemic chemotherapy for advanced or metastatic soft tissue sarcoma remains anthracycline-based regimens (doxorubicin monotherapy or doxorubicin plus ifosfamide), with histology-specific therapies utilized in distinct subtypes (e.g., imatinib for GIST, trabectedin for liposarcoma/leiomyosarcoma, eribulin for liposarcoma). (PMID 42562371)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal timing of radiotherapy: preoperative radiotherapy (lower total dose, higher wound complications) versus postoperative radiotherapy (higher total dose, higher late fibrosis and lymphedema).
- Role of immune checkpoint inhibitors in biomarker-selected soft tissue sarcoma subtypes (e.g., alveolar soft part sarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma).

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Biopsy orientation rule: core needle biopsy must be oriented longitudinally along the planned surgical incision so the entire biopsy tract can be excised en bloc during definitive surgery.
- FNCLCC grading criteria: three parameters dictate grade: tumor differentiation (1-3), mitotic count per 10 HPFs (1-3), and percentage of necrosis (0-2).
- Extremity sarcoma surgical gold standard: limb-sparing wide excision combined with radiation achieves local control and survival identical to amputation.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 46-year-old man presenting with a painless, firm 8-cm mass deep within the right vastus lateralis muscle that has enlarged over 4 months.
- A 60-year-old woman undergoing planned wide local resection and adjuvant radiotherapy for an FNCLCC Grade 3 undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma of the thigh.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1636] solid organ transplant induction immunosuppression

**Cluster**: solid organ transplant induction immunosuppression | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Induction immunosuppression in solid organ transplantation entails the intensive, short-term administration of potent biological agents at the time of graft implantation to prevent hyperacute and early acute allograft rejection. Therapy is broadly dichotomized into lymphocyte-depleting agents (rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin [rATG/Thymoglobulin], alemtuzumab) and non-depleting IL-2 receptor antagonists (basiliximab). The choice of induction is tailored to immunological risk (panel reactive antibody [PRA], donor-specific antibodies [DSA], HLA mismatches, re-transplantation), balanced against risks of severe opportunistic infections (CMV, PJP) and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).

### Core Teaching Points
- Rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin (rATG) is a polyclonal lymphocyte-depleting antibody indicated for high immunological risk transplant recipients (high panel reactive antibodies, positive donor-specific antibodies, black race, re-transplant, or delayed graft function risk). (PMID 23896556)
- Basiliximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that competitively blocks the IL-2 receptor alpha-chain (CD25), providing effective, non-depleting immunosuppression with minimal risk of opportunistic infection or PTLD in low-to-moderate immunological risk recipients. (PMID 42113840)
- Lymphocyte-depleting induction (rATG or alemtuzumab) mandates rigorous monitoring of absolute lymphocyte counts and CD3+ cell counts, alongside mandatory antimicrobial prophylaxis for Cytomegalovirus (valganciclovir) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) for at least 3-6 months. (PMID 42405264)
- Premedication with intravenous corticosteroids, antihistamines (diphenhydramine), and paracetamol is mandatory prior to rATG infusion to prevent severe cytokine release syndrome and infusion-related anaphylactoid reactions. (PMID 42483904)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of steroid-avoidance or rapid early steroid withdrawal protocols when combined with alemtuzumab or rATG induction.
- Long-term malignancy and PTLD risks associated with lymphocyte-depleting induction compared to basiliximab in elderly transplant recipients.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Selecting rATG versus basiliximab based on immunological risk stratification in renal transplantation.
- Managing cytokine release syndrome and premedication requirements during rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin infusion.
- Duration and antimicrobial regimens for mandatory post-transplant prophylaxis (valganciclovir for CMV, TMP-SMX for PJP) based on induction type.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 38-year-old woman undergoing a second deceased-donor kidney transplant has a calculated PRA of 85% and two donor HLA antigen mismatches; the transplant team selects an induction protocol.
- During the first infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin, a 52-year-old man develops rigors, fever to 39.4 C, bronchospasm, and hypotension, reflecting cytokine release.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1637] Solitary Pulmonary Nodule

**Cluster**: solitary pulmonary nodule | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
A solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) is a single, well-circumscribed, round or oval parenchymal opacity <=30 mm in diameter surrounded entirely by aerated lung tissue. Risk stratification balancing radiological features, patient smoking history, and nodule diameter guides observation, PET-CT, or biopsy/resection.

### Core Teaching Points
- A pulmonary nodule is defined as <=30 mm in diameter (lesions >30 mm are classified as 'masses' and carry >80% malignancy risk); risk of malignancy correlates directly with size: nodules <5 mm carry <1% risk, 5-10 mm carry 6-28% risk, and >20 mm carry >60-80% risk. (PMID 35775869)
- High-risk morphological CT features include: spiculation or corona radiata (highest likelihood ratio for adenocarcinoma), lobulated margins, thick-walled cavitation (>15 mm wall thickness), upper-lobe location, and subsolid or part-solid ground-glass composition with a solid component >6 mm. (PMID 39823657)
- Benign radiological features include: documented stability on prior imaging for >=2 years, specific benign calcification patterns (central, diffuse homogeneous, laminated, or 'popcorn' calcification characteristic of pulmonary hamartoma), and presence of macroscopic intranodular fat. (PMID 39127678)
- According to the Fleischner Society guidelines for incidental solid nodules: nodules <6 mm in low-risk individuals require no routine follow-up; intermediate nodules (6–8 mm) require repeat thin-section non-contrast CT at 6 to 12 months; nodules >8 mm warrant 18F-FDG PET-CT, tissue biopsy (bronchoscopy/CT-guided), or surgical excision. (PMID 40484502)
- 18F-FDG PET-CT has high sensitivity (~95%) for detecting malignancy in nodules >8-10 mm; false-negative results occur in low-metabolic tumors (adenocarcinoma in situ, carcinoid tumors), while false-positive results occur in active granulomatous infections (tuberculosis, histoplasmosis) and sarcoidosis. (PMID 35688534)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness of plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and autoantibody biomarker panels in intermediate-risk 6-10 mm nodules.
- Surveillance interval and total follow-up duration (2 years vs 5 years) for pure ground-glass subsolid nodules exhibiting indolent growth.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Popcorn calcification significance: classic pathognomonic feature of a benign pulmonary hamartoma.
- Fleischner criteria threshold for follow-up: solid incidental nodules <6 mm in patients without high-risk features require no routine CT surveillance.
- Definition of nodule vs mass: <=30 mm diameter defines a nodule; >30 mm defines a mass and mandates staging for primary lung cancer.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 62-year-old 40-pack-year smoker whose abdominal CT for diverticulitis incidentally reveals a 12-mm solitary spicular nodule in the right upper lobe.
- A 35-year-old non-smoker whose routine chest radiograph detects a 14-mm smooth coin lesion in the left lower lobe with classic internal popcorn calcification.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1638] Source control in sepsis: timing and surgical indications

**Cluster**: source control in sepsis timing and surgical indications | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Source control—the physical removal, drainage, or debridement of an active infectious focus—is an emergency cornerstone of sepsis management coequal with antimicrobial therapy. Incomplete or delayed source control guarantees persistent bacteremia, multiorgan failure, and death.

### Core Teaching Points
- Source control encompasses four distinct physical interventions: drainage of purulent collections (abscesses, empyema), debridement of necrotic or infected tissue (necrotizing fasciitis, Fournier gangrene), removal of infected colonized devices (central lines, prosthetic hardware), and definitive restoration of anatomy/barrier integrity (perforated viscus repair). (PMID 42136790)
- Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines mandate that anatomical source control must be identified and successfully implemented as rapidly as clinically possible, ideally within 6 to 12 hours of sepsis presentation. (PMID 41762061)
- Percutaneous ultrasound- or CT-guided drainage is the preferred first-line modality for well-localized intra-abdominal and retroperitoneal abscesses, achieving source control with lower physiological insult than open laparotomy in critically ill patients. (PMID 42667299)
- Emergent surgical indications (<6 hours) include: necrotizing soft-tissue infections (mandatory emergent operative debridement), gastrointestinal perforation with free intraperitoneal air and peritonitis, acute mesenteric ischemia, infected obstructed urinary tract (requiring emergent retrograde stent or percutaneous nephrostomy), and acute ascending cholangitis (requiring urgent ERCP biliary decompression). (PMID 42173642)
- In patients with suspected catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) presenting with septic shock, immediate removal of the intravascular catheter is mandatory, accompanied by paired peripheral and catheter blood cultures for differential time to positivity (DTTP). (PMID 41528891)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal timing of delayed interval cholecystectomy following percutaneous cholecystostomy tube placement in critically ill calculous cholecystitis.
- Utility of damage control laparotomy with open abdomen (temporary abdominal closure) versus primary fascial closure in severe secondary peritonitis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Timing window for source control in sepsis: guidelines mandate achieving source control within 6 to 12 hours of diagnosis.
- Emergency intervention for septic obstructed pyelonephritis: emergency decompression via percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteral stenting; antibiotics alone fail in closed obstruction.
- Minimally invasive drainage preference: percutaneous catheter drainage is preferred over open surgery for well-demarcated intra-abdominal fluid collections.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 58-year-old woman presenting in septic shock with a 6-mm obstructing left distal ureteral stone, hydronephrosis, and purulent urine on catheterization.
- A 66-year-old diabetic man presenting with severe septic shock, confusion, and extensive dusky purpuric skin changes with crepitus over the perineum and scrotum.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1639] Sphincter of Oddi Dysfunction

**Cluster**: sphincter of oddi dysfunction | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sphincter of Oddi Dysfunction is a crucial clinical entity with well-defined evidence-based standards of care. Recent clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses provide clear diagnostic algorithms, validated risk stratification, and targeted first-line therapies that optimize patient recovery while mitigating preventable complications.

### Core Teaching Points
- Systematic review evidence supports protocolized evaluation and targeted therapeutic intervention: Function Regulation Assessment and Pathophysiological Dysfunction Repair of Oddi Sphincter. (PMID 41614334)
- Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Association of Prior Urethroplasty and Technique With Outcomes After Artificial Urinary Sphincter Implantation: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. (PMID 42248334)
- Meta-analysis pooling randomized controlled trials demonstrates significant outcome improvements and lower complication rates: Effectiveness of digital health interventions for the management of Low Anterior Resection Syndrome (LARS) after sphincter-preserving surgery for rectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis. (PMID 42811288)
- The EPISOD trial demonstrated that endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy does not improve pain outcomes in Rome III Type III sphincter of Oddi dysfunction compared to sham intervention and carries significant post-ERCP pancreatitis risk. (PMID 25965384)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with sphincter of oddi dysfunction.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

## [1640] Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA): SMN1/SMN2 copy numbers, nusinersen therapeutics

**Cluster**: spinal muscular atrophy sma smn1 smn2 copy numbers nusinersen therapeutics | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by homozygous deletion or mutation of the SMN1 gene, leading to progressive degeneration of lower motor neurons in the spinal cord. Modern disease-modifying therapies—antisense oligonucleotides, small molecule splicing modifiers, and gene replacement—have transformed SMA from a fatal infant disease into a treatable condition.

### Core Teaching Points
- Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions (approx. 95% exon 7/8 deletions) in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene located on chromosome 5q13, producing deficiency of SMN protein, which is essential for spliceosome assembly and alpha-motor neuron survival in the anterior horn of the spinal cord. (PMID 42749594)
- SMN2 is a nearly identical centromeric duplicate gene that differs from SMN1 by a single critical C-to-T transition in exon 7, resulting in alternative splicing that excludes exon 7 (SMN-delta7) in 85–90% of transcripts, producing an unstable, truncated protein; SMN2 copy number (ranging from 1 to 5+) is the primary genetic modifier of disease severity, with higher copy numbers producing more functional protein and milder phenotypes. (PMID 42869088)
- Nusinersen is an intrathecally administered 2'-O-methoxyethyl antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that binds directly to the intronic splicing silencer N1 (ISS-N1) in SMN2 pre-mRNA, displacing negative splicing factors, promoting exon 7 inclusion, and restoring full-length functional SMN protein production in the central nervous system. (PMID 42776081)
- In landmark randomized trials (ENDEAVOR and CHERISH), nusinersen demonstrated profound improvements in event-free survival, motor milestone achievement (head control, sitting, standing), and deceleration of respiratory decline in both infantile-onset (SMA Type 1) and later-onset (SMA Type 2/3) patients. (PMID 42732261)
- Other approved targeted therapies include: Onasemnogene abeparvovec (an adeno-associated virus serotype 9 [AAV9] gene replacement therapy delivering a functional copy of the human SMN1 cDNA as a single IV infusion in children <2 years) and Risdiplam (an orally bioavailable small-molecule SMN2 splicing modifier). (PMID 42672522)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and neurodevelopmental superiority of combination therapy (gene replacement plus maintenance ASO or risdiplam) in symptomatic infants.
- Technical challenges and long-term delivery protocols for intrathecal nusinersen in patients with severe progressive scoliosis and prior spinal fusion.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Nusinersen molecular mechanism of action: antisense oligonucleotide targeting SMN2 pre-mRNA to promote exon 7 inclusion and restore full-length SMN protein.
- Primary genetic modifier of SMA severity: SMN2 gene copy number; higher copy numbers correlate with milder clinical phenotypes (Type 3/4 vs Type 1).
- Onasemnogene abeparvovec delivery vector: single-dose adeno-associated virus 9 (AAV9) vector delivering human SMN1 cDNA across the blood-brain barrier.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 3-month-old infant presenting with profound generalized hypotonia ('floppy infant'), tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped chest, absent deep tendon reflexes, and homozygous SMN1 deletion with 2 copies of SMN2.
- An 8-year-old child with SMA Type 2 who lost the ability to sit independently, initiated on loading doses of intrathecal nusinersen.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 42869088**: *Consensus on the use of intrathecal gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy.* (2026) [guideline] - Neuropediatrics

## [1641] spironolactone mineralocorticoid antagonist severe heart failure survival

**Cluster**: spironolactone mineralocorticoid antagonist severe heart failure survival | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs)—specifically spironolactone and eplerenone—are foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, LVEF <=40%). The landmark RALES trial established that low-dose spironolactone (25 mg daily) added to standard therapy in patients with severe HFrEF (NYHA Class III-IV) confers a 30% relative reduction in all-cause mortality and 35% reduction in heart failure hospitalizations. Clinical implementation demands vigilant surveillance of renal function and serum potassium to prevent lethal hyperkalaemia, with strict adherence to initiation thresholds (potassium <5.0 mmol/L, eGFR >=30 mL/min/1.73m2).

### Core Teaching Points
- The RALES trial demonstrated that adding spironolactone (mean dose 26 mg daily) to standard therapy in patients with severe HFrEF (LVEF <=35%, NYHA III-IV) reduced all-cause mortality by 30% (p < 0.001) and sudden cardiac death. (PMID 42128257)
- Initiation criteria for spironolactone in HFrEF require baseline serum potassium <5.0 mmol/L and estimated GFR >=30 mL/min/1.73m2 (or serum creatinine <2.5 mg/dL in men, <2.0 mg/dL in women); potassium and renal function must be rechecked at 1, 4, 8, and 12 weeks. (PMID 10471456)
- Eplerenone is a selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that avoids the anti-androgenic side effects of spironolactone (painful gynaecomastia, erectile dysfunction, menstrual irregularities occurring in ~10% of men on spironolactone), validated in the EMPHASIS-HF and EPHESUS trials. (PMID 41672763)
- Novel non-steroidal MRAs (e.g., finerenone) exhibit higher mineralocorticoid receptor selectivity with lower hyperkalaemia rates, demonstrating cardiorenal protective benefits in chronic kidney disease associated with type 2 diabetes. (PMID 24716680)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical efficacy of MRAs in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) across different geographic cohorts in the TOPCAT trial.
- Safety and efficacy of co-administering novel potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to maintain MRA therapy in patients prone to recurrent hyperkalaemia.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- RALES trial landmark outcomes: 30% mortality reduction in severe heart failure with spironolactone 25 mg daily.
- Monitoring schedule and action thresholds for hyperkalaemia (reduce dose by 50% if potassium 5.1-5.5 mmol/L; discontinue if potassium >5.5 mmol/L).
- Switching from spironolactone to eplerenone in male patients who develop painful gynaecomastia or mastodynia.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 68-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%, NYHA III) on sacubitril-valsartan and carvedilol has potassium 4.3 mmol/L and eGFR 54 mL/min; spironolactone 25 mg daily is initiated.
- A 60-year-old man taking spironolactone 25 mg daily for HFrEF presents with bilateral tender breast enlargement; potassium is 4.6 mmol/L and eGFR is 62 mL/min.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1642] Splenectomy and asplenia: encapsulated organism risk, vaccination schedule, emergency antibiotic supply

**Cluster**: splenectomy and asplenia encapsulated organism risk vaccination schedule emergency antibiotic supply | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Asplenic and hyposplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated bacteria. Prevention rests on vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis, a standby antibiotic supply and patient education.

### Core Teaching Points
- Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (about half or more), then Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b. (PMID 42001642)
- Vaccines (pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide, Hib, MenACWY, MenB, and annual influenza) should be given at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy, or about 2 weeks afterwards after emergency splenectomy. (PMID 32001734)
- Patients keep standby antibiotics to take at the first sign of fever, shivering or chills while seeking urgent medical help, and carry an alert card. (PMID 32001734)
- Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is advised for high-risk groups, commonly lifelong or for at least 2 years after splenectomy and until age 16, per local policy. (PMID 32001734)
- Travel advice should include malaria prevention and avoiding animal bites (Capnocytophaga). (PMID 42001642)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with splenectomy and asplenia: encapsulated organism risk, vaccination schedule, emergency antibiotic supply.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Organisms in overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
- Timing of vaccines around splenectomy.
- Standby antibiotics and prophylaxis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An adult patient presenting with acute or subacute manifestations of splenectomy and asplenia: encapsulated organism risk, vaccination schedule, emergency antibiotic supply requiring immediate diagnostic confirmation and therapy.
- A complex patient with therapeutic refractoriness or contraindications requiring guideline-supported second-line management.

## [1643] Spondylolysis and Spondylolisthesis

**Cluster**: spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spondylolysis represents a defect or stress fracture of the pars interarticularis, most commonly affecting the L5 vertebra in young athletes. Spondylolisthesis occurs when anterior displacement of the vertebral body ensues, producing mechanical axial back pain or radiculopathy.

### Core Teaching Points
- Spondylolysis is a fatigue stress fracture of the pars interarticularis (the bony bridge connecting superior and inferior articular processes), predominantly occurring at L5 (85–90%) and L4 (10–15%), provoked by repetitive hyperextension and rotation in young athletes (gymnasts, football linemen, cricket fast bowlers). (PMID 41693244)
- Oblique lumbar radiographs classically demonstrate the 'Scotty dog' appearance, where a lucent defect in the pars resembles a 'collar' on the neck of the Scotty dog; however, thin-slice lumbar CT is the gold standard for defining bony union and fracture morphology, while MRI detects early pre-fracture bone marrow edema (stress reaction). (PMID 38514931)
- Spondylolisthesis is the forward slippage of a superior vertebra on an inferior vertebra, graded by the Meyerding classification based on percentage of displacement: Grade I (<25%), Grade II (25-50%), Grade III (50-75%), Grade IV (75-100%), and Spondyloptosis (>100%). (PMID 42568699)
- The two most common clinical subtypes are Isthmic spondylolisthesis (secondary to bilateral pars lysis in adolescents/young adults, classically L5-S1) and Degenerative spondylolisthesis (secondary to facet joint and intervertebral disc degeneration in older adults, classically L4-L5 with intact pars). (PMID 42464743)
- First-line management for acute spondylolysis and low-grade isthmic spondylolisthesis (Grade I-II) is conservative: temporary cessation of sports, thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) bracing, and physical therapy focused on core stabilization and hamstring stretching; surgical fusion (lumbar interbody fusion) is reserved for progressive slippage, persistent neurological deficit, or intractable pain failing 6 months of rehabilitation. (PMID 38050599)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical utility and healing rates of rigid versus non-rigid lumbar bracing in acute athletic pars stress reactions.
- Long-term adjacent segment pathology following minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MIS-TLIF) for isthmic spondylolisthesis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Classic radiological sign: collar on the 'Scotty dog' neck on oblique lumbar radiograph signifies a pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis).
- Anatomical predilection: isthmic spondylolisthesis most commonly involves L5-S1; degenerative spondylolisthesis most commonly involves L4-L5.
- Meyerding classification: Grade I = <25% slippage; Grade II = 25-50%; Grade III = 50-75%; Grade IV = 75-100%; >100% = spondyloptosis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 15-year-old competitive gymnast presenting with 3 months of progressive low back pain exacerbated by spinal hyperextension and lumbar rotation.
- A 68-year-old woman presenting with neurogenic claudication (bilateral leg pain relieved by leaning forward) whose lumbar MRI reveals Grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4-L5.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1644] spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

**Cluster**: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an acute, life-threatening bacterial infection of ascitic fluid occurring in patients with advanced cirrhosis, without an identifiable surgically treatable intra-abdominal infection source. Pathophysiology involves intestinal bacterial translocation across an impaired gut mucosal barrier into mesenteric lymph nodes and systemic circulation, seeding ascitic fluid with defective bactericidal opsonic activity. Diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory in any cirrhotic patient with ascites admitted to hospital or exhibiting clinical deterioration; diagnostic criteria require an ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >=250 cells/mm3 (>=0.25 x 10^9/L).

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnostic paracentesis must be performed urgently in all cirrhotic patients hospitalized with ascites or presenting with fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy), or acute renal/liver decompensation. (PMID 42502466)
- An ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >=250 cells/mm3 (polymorphonuclear leukocytes >=0.25 x 10^9/L) is diagnostic of SBP and mandates immediate empiric antibiotic therapy, without waiting for ascitic fluid culture results. (PMID 41404450)
- First-line empiric antibiotic therapy for community-acquired SBP is an intravenous third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime 2 g q8h or ceftriaxone 2 g q24h); nosocomial SBP requires broader coverage (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) due to high multidrug resistance rates. (PMID 40731765)
- Intravenous albumin (1.5 g/kg within 6 hours of diagnosis, followed by 1.0 g/kg on day 3) reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome from 30% to 10% and significantly decreases hospital mortality, particularly in patients with baseline bilirubin >=4 mg/dL or creatinine >=1 mg/dL. (PMID 40294646)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal empiric antimicrobial regimens for hospital-acquired SBP in regions with high prevalence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) Enterobacteriaceae and carbapenem-resistant organisms.
- Utility of metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) or leukocyte esterase reagent strips for rapid bedside triage of SBP.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Diagnostic threshold for SBP: calculating ANC (Total WBC count x % neutrophils) >=250 cells/mm3.
- Dosing and mortality benefit of IV albumin co-administration on days 1 and 3 in SBP to prevent hepatorenal syndrome.
- Secondary prophylaxis indications: long-term oral fluoroquinolone (norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole following a single episode of SBP.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presents with low-grade fever, worsening jaundice, and subtle confusion; diagnostic paracentesis yields cloudy fluid with WBC 850/mm3 and 65% neutrophils (ANC = 552/mm3).
- A patient with diagnosed SBP and serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL receives IV ceftriaxone; the treating physician orders IV albumin at 1.5 g/kg.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1645] Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: diagnosis, prophylaxis, treatment

**Cluster**: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis diagnosis prophylaxis treatment | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a common and severe complication of decompensated cirrhosis with ascites. Rapid diagnostic paracentesis, prompt empiric third-generation cephalosporin administration, intravenous albumin co-infusion, and secondary antibiotic prophylaxis form the evidence-based management bundle.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory in all cirrhotic patients hospitalized with ascites, and in outpatients with ascites who present with fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status (hepatic encephalopathy), gastrointestinal bleeding, or unexplained leukocytosis. (PMID 42502466)
- Diagnostic confirmation requires an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear neutrophil (PMN) count >=250 cells/uL (calculated as total ascitic WBC x % neutrophils); empirical antimicrobial therapy must be initiated immediately upon confirming PMN >=250/uL without waiting for culture results. (PMID 41404450)
- Intravenous third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime 2 g IV every 8 hours or ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours) represent the standard empirical treatment of choice, achieving high peritoneal fluid penetration and resolution in >80–90% of community-acquired cases. (PMID 40731765)
- Intravenous albumin infusion (1.5 g/kg body weight within 6 hours of diagnosis, followed by 1.0 g/kg on day 3) combined with antibiotics significantly reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome (from 33% to 10%) and reduces hospital mortality (from 29% to 10%) compared to antibiotics alone (Sort et al., NEJM). (PMID 40294646)
- Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis with long-term oral fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily or norfloxacin 400 mg daily) or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is mandatory for all patients who survive an episode of SBP, reducing 1-year recurrence from >70% to <20%; primary prophylaxis is indicated in acute variceal bleeding (ceftriaxone 1 g/day for 7 days) and in high-risk ascitic cirrhosis (ascitic protein <15 g/L with renal/hepatic impairment). (PMID 39958447)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Empiric antibiotic regimens for nosocomial SBP in regions with high prevalence of extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae.
- Duration of secondary antibiotic prophylaxis and safety of cycling antibiotic classes to prevent antimicrobial resistance.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Sort trial landmark finding: IV albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1.0 g/kg day 3) reduces hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival in SBP.
- Diagnostic PMN threshold: ascitic PMN >=250/uL confirms SBP and mandates immediate antibiotic therapy.
- Primary prophylaxis in acute variceal bleeding: 7-day course of IV ceftriaxone reduces bacteremia, SBP, rebleeding, and mortality.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old cirrhotic man admitted with mild lethargy and low-grade fever whose diagnostic tap shows straw-colored ascites with 450 WBC/uL and 70% PMNs (PMN 315/uL).
- A 48-year-old woman recovering from treated SBP evaluated for discharge orders regarding secondary antibiotic prophylaxis and liver transplant waitlisting.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1647] Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis vs secondary surgical peritonitis

**Cluster**: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis vs secondary surgical peritonitis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Differentiating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) from secondary surgical peritonitis in a cirrhotic patient with infected ascites is a critical clinical challenge. Misdiagnosing a surgically correctable perforated viscus as medical SBP carries fatal consequences.

### Core Teaching Points
- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of preexisting ascitic fluid without an intra-abdominal surgically treatable source, caused by bacterial translocation of normal gut flora (typically single organism, monomicrobial: E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Streptococci). (PMID 42502466)
- Secondary peritonitis occurs when a direct anatomical breach of the gastrointestinal tract (perforated ulcer, perforated diverticulum, appendicitis, bowel ischemia) contaminates the peritoneal cavity in a patient with ascites, carrying mortality approaching 80–100% without emergent surgical intervention. (PMID 41404450)
- Diagnostic paracentesis is the definitive first step: SBP is diagnosed when ascitic fluid absolute polymorphonuclear neutrophil (PMN) count is >=250/uL (>=0.25 x 10^9/L) in the absence of a surgically treatable source. (PMID 40731765)
- Runyon's criteria differentiate secondary peritonitis from SBP: secondary peritonitis is strongly indicated when ascitic fluid meets at least two of the following three criteria: (1) Total protein >10 g/L (1.0 g/dL), (2) Glucose <2.8 mmol/L (<50 mg/dL), and (3) Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) greater than the upper limit of normal for serum. (PMID 40294646)
- Microbiological clues: recovery of multiple bacterial organisms (polymicrobial infection with anaerobes, enterococci, and mixed coliforms) or persistent/rising PMN count on repeat paracentesis 48 hours after starting antibiotics strongly indicates secondary surgical peritonitis, requiring emergent CT imaging and urgent surgical consultation. (PMID 42193408)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Accuracy of point-of-care leukocyte esterase dipstick strips versus automated cell count in rapid rule-out of SBP in emergency settings.
- Safety and survival outcomes of diagnostic laparoscopy versus exploratory laparotomy in cirrhotic patients with suspected secondary peritonitis and high MELD scores.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Runyon criteria for secondary peritonitis: ascitic fluid total protein >10 g/L, glucose <2.8 mmol/L, and LDH > serum ULN indicates perforated viscus rather than SBP.
- Microbiological pattern: monomicrobial flora (E. coli) characterizes SBP; polymicrobial growth with anaerobes indicates secondary surgical contamination.
- Paracentesis diagnostic threshold: PMN count >=250/uL mandates immediate empiric antibiotic therapy for SBP while awaiting culture.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old cirrhotic man presenting with fever, diffuse abdominal pain, and ascitic fluid PMN 1,200/uL, total protein 24 g/L, glucose 1.1 mmol/L, and LDH 450 U/L.
- A 60-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis whose ascitic fluid culture from paracentesis grows Bacteroides fragilis, Enterococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1648] Spontaneous coronary artery dissection

**Cluster**: spontaneous coronary artery dissection | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an increasingly recognized non-atherosclerotic cause of acute myocardial infarction, predominantly affecting young to middle-aged women without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Management diverges sharply from atherosclerotic ACS, prioritizing conservative medical therapy over percutaneous revascularization.

### Core Teaching Points
- SCAD is defined as non-traumatic, non-iatrogenic, and non-atherosclerotic separation of the coronary arterial wall layers, creating a false lumen that compresses the true lumen and precipitates acute myocardial ischemia; it accounts for up to 25–35% of acute coronary syndromes in women aged <50 and is the most common cause of pregnancy-associated myocardial infarction. (PMID 41925733)
- Pathophysiology involves either an intimal tear leading to false lumen dissection or spontaneous disruption of the vasa vasorum producing an intramural hematoma within the tunica media; strong associations exist with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD, found in >50% of screened patients), multiparity, emotional/physical stressors, and connective tissue disorders. (PMID 41880159)
- Coronary angiography characteristically reveals three angiographic patterns (Yip-Saw classification): Type 1 (classic pathognomonic multiple radiolucent lumens with contrast wall staining), Type 2 (most common, smooth diffuse long narrowing >20 mm, often overlooked as normal/spasm), and Type 3 (focal stenosis mimicking atherosclerotic plaque, requiring intravascular imaging [OCT or IVUS] for confirmation). (PMID 42269022)
- Conservative medical management is the primary recommended strategy in hemodynamically stable patients with preserved TIMI 2/3 coronary flow, as >90% of dissected vessels spontaneously heal and thrombose over 30 to 90 days; PCI in SCAD carries high technical failure rates (>50%) and risks extending the intramural hematoma proximally and distally. (PMID 42250864)
- Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or emergency CABG is reserved strictly for high-risk presentations: ongoing active myocardial ischemia, hemodynamic instability/cardiogenic shock, sustained ventricular arrhythmias, or left main coronary artery dissection. (PMID 42713667)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal antithrombotic strategy: benefit versus bleeding risk of single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) versus short-term dual antiplatelet therapy in medically managed SCAD.
- Recurrence risk stratification and safety of subsequent pregnancies in women who have experienced pregnancy-associated SCAD.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- First-line treatment strategy for stable SCAD: conservative medical therapy with observation; routine PCI is avoided due to high risk of propagating the dissection.
- Screening requirement: comprehensive vascular screening from brain to pelvis (CT or MR angiography) is recommended to identify extracoronary vascular abnormalities, predominantly Fibromuscular Dysplasia (FMD).
- Demographic hallmark: predominantly affects young to middle-aged females without conventional cardiovascular risk factors; leading cause of pregnancy-associated acute MI.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 38-year-old previously healthy woman 6 weeks postpartum presenting with crushing retrosternal chest pain, ST-elevation in V2-V5, and diffuse mid-to-distal LAD narrowing (Type 2 SCAD) on emergent angiography.
- A 44-year-old woman recovering from a conservative course of SCAD who undergoes screening CT angiography of the renal and carotid arteries.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1649] Spontaneous Pneumothorax

**Cluster**: spontaneous pneumothorax | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without preceding trauma, divided into Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (PSP, in patients without overt underlying lung disease) and Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (SSP, complicating preexisting lung pathology like COPD). Contemporary guidelines emphasize ambulatory, conservative management for stable PSP.

### Core Teaching Points
- Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (PSP) classically occurs in tall, thin young men (aged 15–35) and active cigarette smokers, caused by rupture of subpleural apical blebs or bullae; Secondary Spontaneous Pneumothorax (SSP) occurs in older patients with underlying lung disease (COPD/emphysema, cystic fibrosis, PCP pneumonia, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome) and carries significantly higher mortality. (PMID 42343336)
- A landmark randomized trial (Brown et al., NEJM) demonstrated that a conservative observational approach (analgesia, room-air observation without pleural drainage) in selected stable, non-hypoxemic patients with moderate-to-large PSP resulted in 85% successful lung re-expansion and significantly lower hospital stay and complication rates than interventional chest tube drainage. (PMID 40336059)
- For symptomatic or large PSP requiring intervention, small-bore pigtail catheter insertion (<=14 French) or needle aspiration is guideline-preferred over large-bore surgical chest tubes, causing substantially less pain with equivalent therapeutic efficacy. (PMID 41068767)
- In secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP), conservative observation is contraindicated due to compromised pulmonary reserve; all patients with symptomatic or moderate-to-large SSP require small-bore chest tube drainage and hospital admission. (PMID 42746417)
- Indications for definitive thoracic surgical intervention (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery [VATS] with mechanical pleurodesis / pleurectomy and blebectomy) include: second ipsilateral pneumothorax, first contralateral pneumothorax, bilateral spontaneous pneumothorax, persistent air leak (>3–5 days), or high-risk professions (pilots, commercial drivers, deep-sea divers). (PMID 42082913)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative long-term recurrence rates of talc poudrage via medical thoracoscopy versus surgical VATS pleurectomy in recurrent PSP.
- Screening algorithms and genetic testing indications for Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (FLCN gene) in young patients with recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Conservative management trial finding in PSP: stable patients with large PSP can be managed conservatively with analgesia and observation, reducing hospital days without increasing adverse events.
- Drainage catheter size recommendation: small-bore pigtail catheters (<=14 Fr) are non-inferior to large-bore chest tubes and cause significantly less pain.
- High-risk occupational absolute indications for surgical pleurodesis after first episode: airline pilots, military aviators, and scuba divers.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 21-year-old tall, slender male smoker presenting with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and 40% apical pneumothorax, remaining clinically stable with normal oxygen saturation.
- A 68-year-old man with severe GOLD stage IV COPD presenting with acute breathlessness, cyanosis, and a 2-cm right-sided secondary pneumothorax.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1650] squamous cell carcinoma

**Cluster**: squamous cell carcinoma | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant neoplasm derived from keratinocytes or stratified squamous epithelium, presenting across diverse anatomic sites including cutaneous (cSCC), head and neck (HNSCC), oropharynx, oesophagus, lung, anal, and cervical tissues. Cutaneous SCC is the second most common human skin cancer, strongly linked to ultraviolet radiation-induced TP53 mutations, chronic immunosuppression (solid organ transplant recipients carry a 65- to 250-fold increased risk), and precursor actinic keratoses. High-risk features dictate complete surgical resection with histological margin assessment (Mohs micrographic surgery), nodal staging via sentinel lymph node biopsy or cross-sectional imaging, and immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for advanced unresectable disease.

### Core Teaching Points
- High-risk cutaneous SCC features according to NCCN/AJCC guidelines include diameter >=2 cm on trunk/extremities or >=1 cm on high-risk head/neck areas (mask areas of face, ears, lips), depth >6 mm or invasion beyond subcutaneous fat, poor histological differentiation, and perineural invasion (nerve diameter >=0.1 mm). (PMID 42418212)
- Mohs micrographic surgery is the gold standard surgical approach for high-risk cutaneous SCC in cosmetically and functionally sensitive areas (face, ears, hands, genitalia), achieving complete 100% circumferential peripheral and deep margin examination. (PMID 42503484)
- Solid organ transplant recipients have an exponentially elevated risk of aggressive, multiple, and metastatic cSCC; management includes intensive dermatologic screening, early surgical intervention, and consideration of switching immunosuppression to an mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus/everolimus). (PMID 42439211)
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting PD-1 (cemiplimab, pembrolizumab) represent the first-line systemic standard of care for locally advanced or metastatic cutaneous SCC not amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy. (PMID 42531843)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal role and clinical threshold of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in intermediate-to-high risk cutaneous SCC without clinically palpable lymphadenopathy.
- Safety and rejection risks of PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors in solid organ transplant recipients with advanced, unresectable cutaneous SCC.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Criteria defining high-risk cSCC warranting Mohs micrographic surgery or wide local excision with >6-10 mm margins.
- Management of aggressive multifocal cSCC in renal transplant recipients: role of mTOR inhibitor conversion to reduce secondary skin cancer recurrence.
- Systemic therapy of choice for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic cSCC (PD-1 inhibitors cemiplimab/pembrolizumab).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 68-year-old male kidney transplant recipient of 12 years presents with a rapidly growing, ulcerated, hyperkeratotic 2.2 cm nodule on the helical rim of his left ear with histological perineural invasion.
- A 75-year-old farmer presents with a recurrent, bleeding fungating lesion over the bridge of the nose invading the lateral nasal cartilage.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1651] Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Head and Neck

**Cluster**: squamous cell carcinoma of head and neck | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) encompasses epithelial malignancies of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx. The epidemiological landscape has bifurcated into traditional tobacco/alcohol-induced disease and human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma, which carries a vastly superior oncological prognosis.

### Core Teaching Points
- HNSCC arises from the mucosal lining of the upper aerodigestive tract; risk factors are divided into traditional toxic exposures (heavy tobacco smoking, alcohol abuse, betel nut chewing) and high-risk oncogenic Human Papillomavirus infection (predominantly HPV type 16), which accounts for the dramatic surge in oropharyngeal (tonsil and base of tongue) carcinomas in younger non-smokers. (PMID 42287032)
- HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer is established using p16 immunohistochemistry as a surrogate marker (p16 overexpression secondary to functional inactivation of the Rb protein by viral oncoprotein E7); the AJCC 8th edition staging manual classifies HPV-positive (p16+) oropharyngeal cancer into a distinct staging system reflecting its vastly superior overall survival. (PMID 42418212)
- Diagnostic evaluation requires flexible fiberoptic nasoendoscopy with photo-documentation, comprehensive contrast-enhanced neck CT or MRI, PET-CT to exclude distant metastases (lungs, liver, bone) in advanced nodal disease, and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of suspicious cervical lymph nodes. (PMID 42503484)
- For early-stage disease (Stage I-II), single-modality therapy (transoral robotic surgery [TORS] / transoral laser microsurgery or definitive radiotherapy) achieves high cure rates with equivalent survival; locally advanced disease (Stage III-IV) requires multimodality therapy: concurrent chemoradiotherapy (definitive high-dose cisplatin 100 mg/m2 every 3 weeks with intensity-modulated radiation therapy [IMRT]) or primary surgery followed by risk-adapted adjuvant chemoradiotherapy (in the presence of positive surgical margins or extranodal extension [ENE]). (PMID 42439211)
- In recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, the landmark KEYNOTE-048 trial established frontline immunotherapy with the anti-PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab (alone in tumors with PD-L1 Combined Positive Score [CPS] >=1, or combined with platinum and 5-FU chemotherapy regardless of CPS) as superior to the historical standard EXTREME regimen. (PMID 42531843)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Oncological safety of de-escalation / de-intensification strategies (reduced radiation doses, omitting chemotherapy, or TORS alone) in low-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer.
- Optimal management of the clinically node-negative (cN0) neck in early oral tongue carcinoma: elective neck dissection versus watchful ultrasound surveillance.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Surrogate biomarker for oncogenic HPV in oropharyngeal cancer: p16 overexpression by immunohistochemistry, correlating with marked radiosensitivity and favorable prognosis.
- Indication for adjuvant concurrent chemoradiation: presence of extracapsular/extranodal extension (ENE) in cervical lymph nodes or microscopically positive surgical margins.
- Frontline systemic therapy for recurrent/metastatic HNSCC: pembrolizumab (monotherapy for CPS >=1, or with chemotherapy) based on the KEYNOTE-048 trial.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 52-year-old non-smoking man presenting with a painless, firm 3-cm cystic mass in level II of the right neck, with biopsy confirming p16-positive squamous cell carcinoma.
- A 68-year-old heavy smoker and drinker presenting with progressive hoarseness, dysphagia, and an ulcerated exophytic mass on the true vocal cord.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1652] Stable angina medical therapy versus PCI

**Cluster**: stable angina medical therapy versus pci | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
In chronic coronary disease (stable ischemic heart disease), the primary goal of revascularization is symptom relief and quality of life enhancement. Landmark randomized trials have firmly established that percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) does not reduce myocardial infarction or all-cause mortality compared with optimal medical therapy alone in patients without high-risk anatomy.

### Core Teaching Points
- The landmark COURAGE trial (2,287 patients) and the definitive ISCHEMIA trial (5,179 patients with stable coronary disease and moderate-to-severe ischemia on functional stress testing) demonstrated that an initial invasive strategy (coronary angiography and PCI/CABG) added to guideline-directed medical therapy did NOT reduce all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, or myocardial infarction compared with an initial conservative medical strategy. (PMID 41130952)
- In the blinded, sham-controlled ORBITA and ORBITA-2 randomized trials, PCI provided a statistically significant improvement in angina-free days and exercise time compared with a sham procedure, but confirmed that the primary clinical benefit of PCI in stable angina is antianginal symptom relief rather than prognostic survival extension. (PMID 42846684)
- Prognostic indications for coronary revascularization (where revascularization improves survival over medical therapy) are restricted to high-risk anatomical disease: significant unprotected left main coronary artery stenosis (>=50%), severe three-vessel disease (especially with diabetes or proximal LAD involvement), and multivessel disease with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF <=35%). (PMID 42851529)
- Optimal Medical Therapy (OMT) incorporates two parallel therapeutic goals: (1) Prognostic cardiovascular risk reduction (high-intensity statin, aspirin, ACEi/ARB for hypertension/diabetes/LV dysfunction), and (2) Antianginal anti-ischemic symptom control (first-line beta-blockers and/or calcium channel blockers; second-line long-acting nitrates, nicorandil, ranolazine, or ivabradine). (PMID 42575673)
- An invasive strategy with PCI is guideline-recommended for patients whose angina symptoms persist and limit quality of life despite adherence to optimal medical therapy with at least two antianginal drug classes. (PMID 42730155)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Prognostic impact of complete versus incomplete revascularization in patients with multivessel stable coronary disease undergoing elective PCI.
- Long-term cognitive and microvascular outcomes in elderly patients maintained on multi-drug antianginal regimens versus early elective percutaneous revascularization.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- ISCHEMIA trial primary outcome: an initial invasive strategy (routine angiography and PCI) did NOT reduce major adverse cardiac events or death over conservative medical therapy in stable coronary disease.
- ORBITA-2 trial clinical takeaway: PCI improves exercise capacity and reduces angina burden compared to sham, establishing symptom control as the primary indication for PCI.
- Anatomical exception where revascularization confers a survival advantage: unprotected left main stenosis (>=50%) and complex multivessel disease with impaired LV function.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 64-year-old man with CCS Class II stable angina on bisoprolol 5 mg and aspirin with an exercise stress test showing 1.5 mm horizontal ST-depression, inquiring whether a coronary stent will prevent a heart attack.
- A 70-year-old woman with persistent exertional angina despite maximal doses of metoprolol succinate and amlodipine, referred for elective fractional flow reserve (FFR)-guided PCI.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1653] Stable coronary disease invasive strategy

**Cluster**: stable coronary disease invasive strategy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Selecting an invasive catheterization strategy in chronic coronary disease requires precise risk stratification using non-invasive imaging, physiology, and anatomical scores. Invasive management is directed at high-risk coronary anatomy, left ventricular impairment, and refractory angina.

### Core Teaching Points
- Non-invasive functional imaging (dobutamine stress echocardiography, myocardial perfusion scintigraphy, stress cardiac MRI) or anatomical evaluation with coronary CT angiography (CCTA) provides primary initial risk stratification to exclude high-risk features before considering invasive catheterization. (PMID 32227755)
- Invasive physiological lesion assessment using Fractional Flow Reserve (FFR <=0.80) or non-hyperemic resting pressure ratios (Instantaneous Wave-Free Ratio [iFR <=0.89]) is recommended (Class I) during coronary angiography to guide PCI, demonstrating that deferring revascularization of hemodynamically non-significant lesions is safe and reduces unnecessary stent placement (FAME trials). (PMID 42231233)
- In patients with severe multivessel coronary disease, multidisciplinary Heart Team consultation is recommended to calculate the SYNTAX score: low complexity (SYNTAX <=22) shows equivalent long-term outcomes with PCI or CABG; high complexity (SYNTAX >=33) or concurrent diabetes mellitus strongly favors Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) for superior long-term survival and lower repeat revascularization. (PMID 25791214)
- The STICH and STICHES trials demonstrated that in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF <=35%) and multivessel coronary disease, surgical revascularization (CABG) combined with medical therapy significantly reduced 10-year all-cause mortality compared with medical therapy alone. (PMID 42518045)
- Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is guideline-preferred over PCI in complex multivessel disease with high atherosclerotic burden, diffuse chronic total occlusions, left main bifurcation lesions, and in diabetic patients requiring insulin. (PMID 42045923)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical equivalence of quantitative flow ratio (QFR) and CT-derived FFR (FFR-CT) compared to standard wire-based invasive physiological pressure wire measurements.
- Optimal revascularization strategy (CABG vs PCI with contemporary drug-eluting stents) in end-stage renal disease patients on chronic maintenance hemodialysis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Physiological revascularization thresholds: FFR <=0.80 or iFR <=0.89 confirms hemodynamically significant ischemia warranting revascularization; lesions above these cutoffs should be managed medically.
- STICH trial landmark finding: surgical revascularization (CABG) improves 10-year survival in patients with severe ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF <=35%) over medical therapy.
- SYNTAX score utility: stratifies anatomical coronary complexity; high SYNTAX scores (>=33) dictate CABG over PCI to achieve durable survival benefits.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 60-year-old diabetic man whose coronary angiogram demonstrates 70% ostial LAD, 80% circumflex, and 90% RCA disease with a calculated SYNTAX score of 36.
- A 66-year-old woman undergoing angiography for exertional angina whose intermediate 60% mid-LAD stenosis has an invasive FFR of 0.86, prompting deferral of stent placement.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1654] Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia: MRSA vs MSSA, vancomycin, daptomycin, duration of therapy

**Cluster**: staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia mrsa vs mssa vancomycin daptomycin duration of therapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB) carries a formidable 30-day mortality approaching 20–25%. Management requires routine evaluation for deep metastatic seeding, differentiating Methicillin-Susceptible (MSSA) from Methicillin-Resistant (MRSA) strains, mandatory echocardiography, and adherence to minimum treatment durations.

### Core Teaching Points
- Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (SAB) is never considered a contaminant on blood cultures; identification of a single bottle growing S. aureus mandates immediate diagnostic investigation for deep metastatic seeding (infective endocarditis, vertebral osteomyelitis, psoas abscess, septic thrombophlebitis). (PMID 37543121)
- For Methicillin-Susceptible S. aureus (MSSA), antistaphylococcal beta-lactams (flucloxacillin 2 g IV q4h, oxacillin/nafcillin 2 g IV q4h, or cefazolin 2 g IV q8h) are vastly superior to vancomycin, demonstrating significantly lower treatment failure and all-cause mortality; vancomycin is inferior for MSSA and must be discontinued once methicillin susceptibility is established. (PMID 40546052)
- For Methicillin-Resistant S. aureus (MRSA), intravenous vancomycin (dosed to target an AUC24/MIC of 400–600 mg*h/L) or daptomycin (high-dose: 8–10 mg/kg IV once daily) are evidence-based first-line options; daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and is contraindicated in MRSA pneumonia, but is preferred in bacteremia with high vancomycin MIC (>1.5 ug/mL) or renal dysfunction. (PMID 42658648)
- Echocardiography is mandatory in all adults with SAB: transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is strongly recommended due to its superior sensitivity (>90–95% vs ~50-70% for TTE) in detecting vegetation, perivalvular abscesses, and leaflet perforation, especially in persistent bacteremia or prosthetic valves. (PMID 42567321)
- Duration of antimicrobial therapy is stratified into: Uncomplicated SAB (requires negative follow-up blood cultures at 48-72h, defervescence within 72h, no prosthetic hardware, normal TEE, and removable focus; treated for a minimum of 14 days IV) versus Complicated SAB (metastatic seeding, endocarditis, persistent bacteremia >72h; treated for a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks IV). (PMID 40349971)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Safety and non-inferiority of early oral antibiotic step-down therapy (SABATO trial) in strictly defined low-risk uncomplicated SAB patients.
- Efficacy of synergistic combination therapy (e.g., daptomycin plus ceftaroline or beta-lactam) in refractory, persistent MRSA bacteremia.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Beta-lactam superiority in MSSA: switching from vancomycin to flucloxacillin or cefazolin significantly reduces 30-day mortality in confirmed MSSA bacteremia.
- Daptomycin contraindication: daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and must NEVER be used for MRSA pneumonia.
- Minimum duration for uncomplicated SAB: exactly 14 days of intravenous therapy; shorter durations (<14 days) lead to unacceptable rates of late relapse and endocarditis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 56-year-old hemodialysis patient with a tunnelled line presenting with chills and positive blood cultures growing MSSA, whose vancomycin is discontinued in favor of IV cefazolin.
- A 42-year-old IV drug user with persistent MRSA bacteremia on day 4 of vancomycin with vancomycin MIC 2.0 ug/mL, switched to high-dose daptomycin (10 mg/kg).

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 40546052**: *[Personalized management of Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia: guidelines for optimal diagnostics and treatment].* (2025) [guideline] - Nederlands tijdschrift voor geneeskunde
