## [1678] Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: diagnosis and treatment

**Cluster**: sudden sensorineural hearing loss diagnosis and treatment | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) is an otolaryngological emergency characterized by rapid-onset sensorineural hearing impairment developing within 72 hours. Immediate clinical diagnosis and urgent initiation of high-dose corticosteroids within the initial therapeutic window dictate recovery.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnostic criteria for SSNHL require sensorineural hearing loss of >=30 decibels (dB) affecting at least three contiguous audiometric frequencies, developing over a period of <=72 hours; it is predominantly unilateral (98%) and idiopathic in >90% of cases. (PMID 42871297)
- Emergency bedside tuning fork assessment: Weber test lateralizes to the UNAFFECTED normal ear (indicating sensorineural loss in the affected ear), and Rinne test demonstrates air conduction greater than bone conduction (AC > BC, positive Rinne) bilaterally, ruling out conductive cerumen impaction or middle ear effusion. (PMID 42531678)
- High-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy is the mainstay of treatment, initiated as early as possible within 2 weeks of symptom onset: oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day, typically 60 mg daily for 7 to 14 days followed by a taper) promotes resolution by reducing cochlear edema and microvascular inflammation. (PMID 42861443)
- Intratympanic (IT) corticosteroid injections (dexamethasone or methylprednisolone injected through the tympanic membrane into the middle ear) achieve high perilymph concentrations without systemic side effects; IT steroids are recommended as salvage therapy for incomplete recovery after systemic steroids or as primary therapy in patients with contraindications to systemic steroids (uncontrolled diabetes, severe hypertension). (PMID 42767670)
- Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and internal auditory canals (IACs) is mandatory in all patients with confirmed SSNHL to rule out a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma, found in 2–5% of SSNHL cases), stroke, or demyelinating disease. (PMID 42137571)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Additive therapeutic benefit of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) combined with corticosteroids versus corticosteroids alone in severe profound SSNHL.
- Prognostic significance of initial audiogram configuration (upsloping low-frequency loss carrying superior recovery vs flat/downsloping profound loss).

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Tuning fork findings in unilateral sensorineural hearing loss: Weber test lateralizes to the normal opposite ear; Rinne test is positive (AC > BC) in both ears.
- Therapeutic window for corticosteroids: maximal recovery occurs when systemic corticosteroids are initiated within 72 hours to 14 days of symptom onset; efficacy declines sharply after 2–4 weeks.
- Mandatory imaging modality: contrast-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals is required to rule out vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 46-year-old man who wakes up with complete loss of hearing, fullness, and high-pitched tinnitus in his left ear with a normal otoscopic examination.
- A 60-year-old diabetic woman with acute left SSNHL whose hearing fails to improve after 10 days of oral prednisone, evaluated for salvage intratympanic dexamethasone injections.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42531678**: *Beyond steroid monotherapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of combination therapy for severe to profound sudden sensorineural hearing loss.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Brazilian journal of otorhinolaryngology
- **PMID 42861443**: *Effectiveness of Intratympanic Steroid Injection on Hearing Threshold Improvement in Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss: A Meta-Analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Journal of audiology & otology

## [1679] Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP): risk factors, patient counselling

**Cluster**: sudden unexpected death in epilepsy sudep risk factors patient counselling | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP) is the leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality, defined as the non-traumatic, non-drowning sudden death of an individual with epilepsy with or without evidence of a seizure. Transparent patient counseling, optimizing seizure control, and nocturnal supervision are life-saving.

### Core Teaching Points
- SUDEP is defined as a sudden, unexpected, witnessed or unwitnessed, non-traumatic, and non-drowning death in a patient with epilepsy, with or without evidence of an antecedent seizure, where post-mortem examination does not reveal a toxicological or anatomical cause of death. (PMID 42839771)
- The single greatest modifiable risk factor for SUDEP is the frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS): patients experiencing >=3 GTCS per year have a >15-fold increased risk of SUDEP compared to seizure-free individuals. (PMID 42134111)
- Major secondary risk factors include: nocturnal seizures, sleeping alone/unsupervised, prone sleeping position ('face-down' post-ictal suffocation), early age of epilepsy onset, long disease duration, and poor adherence to antiseizure medications (ASMs). (PMID 42205872)
- The proposed terminal pathophysiological mechanism (MORTEMUS study) involves a post-ictal sequence: a generalized convulsive seizure triggers post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES), followed by central hypopnea/apnea, bradyarrhythmia or asystole, and secondary terminal cardiac arrest. (PMID 41689717)
- Counseling and preventive strategies: transparent counseling regarding SUDEP is recommended by guidelines (NICE, AAN); the primary prevention is maximizing seizure control to abolish GTCS, promoting medication adherence, avoiding sleep deprivation and excess alcohol, utilizing nocturnal supervision/monitors, and avoiding prone sleep posturing. (PMID 42663317)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical efficacy of wearable smartwatch/accelerometer seizure detection devices in reducing true SUDEP incidence through prompt caregiver alerting.
- Role of adjunctive selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in mitigating post-ictal respiratory depression and central apnea.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Single strongest modifiable risk factor for SUDEP: frequency of generalized tonic-clonic seizures (GTCS); complete control of GTCS dramatically reduces SUDEP risk.
- Post-ictal sleep position hazard: prone sleeping position is found in >70% of unwitnessed SUDEP cases, contributing to post-ictal suffocation and respiratory arrest.
- Guideline communication standard: clinicians should discuss SUDEP early with patients and families to emphasize the critical importance of antiseizure medication adherence.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 22-year-old university student with refractory juvenile myoclonic epilepsy experiencing 4 nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizures per year while living alone in a dormitory.
- A 16-year-old newly diagnosed with focal epilepsy with secondary generalization whose parents inquire about nocturnal seizure alarms and safety.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 42134111**: *Neuromodulation and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy: A systematic review of SUDEP rates across VNS, DBS, and RNS therapies.* (2026) [systematic review] - Seizure

## [1680] suicide risk assessment

**Cluster**: suicide risk assessment | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Suicide risk assessment is a mandatory core clinical competency across all medical, psychiatric, and emergency specialties. Suicide risk formulation has evolved from crude, inaccurate categorical risk categorization ('low, medium, high') to personalized, dynamic, collaborative risk formulation and safety planning. Key clinical components include distinguishing suicidal ideation from intent and plan, evaluating accessible lethal means, identifying modifiable risk factors (major depression, bipolar disorder, substance misuse, severe agitation), and recognizing evidence-based anti-suicidal pharmacotherapies (lithium, clozapine).

### Core Teaching Points
- Asking directly and empathetically about suicidal thoughts, intent, and plans does NOT induce or increase suicidal ideation or behaviour; rather, it reduces distress and opens essential therapeutic dialogue. (PMID 42765379)
- Categorical risk prediction tools and rating scales cannot accurately predict individual suicidal behaviour and should never be used in isolation to determine hospital admission or discharge decisions. (PMID 42710221)
- Lethal means restriction—specifically securing firearms, safe disposal of toxic medications, and bridge barriers—is the single most effective public health and clinical intervention for reducing suicide deaths. (PMID 42179226)
- Lithium in bipolar disorder and major depression, and clozapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia spectrum disorders, are the only psychotropic medications with robust randomized evidence demonstrating specific long-term reduction in suicide and suicide attempts. (PMID 41669103)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Short-term versus long-term anti-suicidal efficacy of rapid-acting interventions such as intravenous ketamine and intranasal esketamine in acute emergency department presentations.
- Reliability and ethical governance of artificial intelligence and electronic health record predictive algorithms for automated suicide risk detection.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Evidence-based anti-suicidal properties of lithium in mood disorders and clozapine in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
- The role of the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (collaborative personalized coping strategies and emergency contacts) over ineffective 'no-suicide contracts'.
- Emergency psychiatric evaluation: identifying imminent warning signs (active preparatory acts, explicit suicide notes, saying goodbyes, sudden calm after severe depression).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 22-year-old college student with severe depression tells the triage nurse she has collected 60 acetaminophen tablets in her drawer and researched lethal dosages online.
- A 35-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has had three serious suicide attempts during depressive episodes; the psychiatric team discusses mood-stabilizing maintenance to reduce long-term suicide risk.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 42765379**: *Comparing lithium and valproate in reducing suicide risk: A territory-wide retrospective cohort study with pairwise and network meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Psychological medicine
- **PMID 42710221**: *Effect of dopamine partial agonist antipsychotics on suicide risk in persons with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - Schizophrenia research

## [1681] Suicide risk assessment and self-harm

**Cluster**: suicide risk assessment and self harm | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Suicide risk assessment requires an empathic, structured clinical interview to evaluate intent, identify psychiatric and situational risk factors, and co-design a personalized safety plan. Moving beyond simplistic risk stratification checklists improves clinical engagement and patient safety.

### Core Teaching Points
- Evidence-based guidelines (NICE, APA) explicitly advise against utilizing actuarial or numerical risk categorization tools (e.g., categorizing patients into 'low', 'medium', or 'high' risk) to guide clinical management, as these tools have unacceptable false-negative rates and fail to predict completed suicide. (PMID 42566567)
- A comprehensive clinical risk formulation systematically evaluates: suicidal ideation (frequency, intensity, duration), specific plan and lethal feasibility, preparatory behaviors (acquiring means, writing notes, giving away belongings), and degree of suicidal intent versus ambivalence. (PMID 42390862)
- Self-harm (non-suicidal self-injury [NSSI] vs suicide attempts) must be differentiated: NSSI is typically performed to regulate overwhelming negative affect, alleviate distress, or express emotional pain without intent to die; however, chronic NSSI is a powerful independent longitudinal risk factor for future suicide attempts. (PMID 42217636)
- The Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is an evidence-based clinical tool comprising six sequential steps: identifying personalized warning signs, internal coping strategies, social contacts/distractions, trusted family/friends for support, professional crisis services, and making the environment safe (restricting access to lethal means). (PMID 42765379)
- Pharmacological interventions with proven, specific antisuicidal properties include: Lithium in bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder (reduces suicide attempts and completed suicides by >60%), Clozapine in schizophrenia (the only FDA-approved antipsychotic for reducing suicidal behavior), and rapid-acting subanesthetic ketamine/esketamine for acute depressive crises. (PMID 42710221)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Long-term real-world effectiveness of digital smartphone safety-planning applications versus physical paper-based safety plans in reducing crisis readmissions.
- Clinical thresholds for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) in acute suicidal crises with psychotic depression.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Psychiatric medication with proven antisuicidal properties in mood disorders: Lithium significantly reduces completed suicide rates independent of its antidepressant maintenance efficacy.
- Clozapine unique regulatory indication: the only antipsychotic with a specific FDA indication for reducing suicidal behavior in schizophrenia.
- Guideline consensus on risk scales: numeric risk stratification scales should not be used to determine admission or discharge; clinical risk formulation and safety planning are required.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder presenting to the emergency department after superficial forearm cutting following abandonment by her partner.
- A 50-year-old man with severe major depression and active suicidal intent who recently purchased a firearm, evaluated for emergency involuntary inpatient psychiatric stabilization.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1682] Superficial Thrombophlebitis versus DVT

**Cluster**: superficial thrombophlebitis versus dvt | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Superficial vein thrombosis (SVT / superficial thrombophlebitis) was historically considered a benign localized condition, but is now recognized as part of the venous thromboembolism (VTE) spectrum. Accurately distinguishing SVT from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and evaluating for concurrent deep propagation is essential.

### Core Teaching Points
- Superficial vein thrombosis (SVT) presents with localized pain, erythema, tenderness, and a palpable, tender, indurated subcutaneous 'cord' along the anatomical course of a superficial vein (most commonly the great saphenous vein [GSV]); deep vein thrombosis (DVT) typically presents with diffuse unilateral calf or whole-leg swelling, edema, and calf tenderness without a visible superficial cord. (PMID 39047307)
- Comprehensive duplex venous ultrasonography of the entire lower extremity is mandatory in all patients with suspected SVT to measure the exact thrombus length and rule out concurrent deep vein thrombosis, which is present in 20–25% of patients presenting with apparent isolated SVT. (PMID 42147034)
- In patients with isolated lower extremity SVT that is >=5 cm in length and located >=3 cm from the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) or saphenopopliteal junction (SPJ), the landmark CALISTO randomized trial established that subcutaneous fondaparinux (2.5 mg once daily for 45 days) significantly reduces the composite of death, PE, DVT, or SVT extension by 85% without increasing major bleeding. (PMID 41758231)
- SVT extending within 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction or saphenopopliteal junction carries high risk of embolization and is classified as equivalent to deep vein thrombosis, mandating full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation (DOACs or therapeutic LMWH) for at least 3 months. (PMID 41177896)
- Migratory or recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis in atypical sites without varicose veins (Trousseau syndrome) is a classic paraneoplastic manifestation of occult visceral adenocarcinoma (pancreatic, gastric, lung, or ovarian malignancy) or underlying systemic vasculitis (Behcet disease, Buerger disease). (PMID 42273726)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and safety of direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) compared to fondaparinux in isolated lower limb SVT (SURPRISE trial extrapolation).
- Indications for thrombophilia screening in young patients presenting with unprovoked, recurrent superficial vein thrombosis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- CALISTO trial regimen for extensive SVT: prophylactic-dose fondaparinux (2.5 mg daily for 45 days) is the evidence-based treatment for isolated SVT >=5 cm in length.
- SVT within 3 cm of saphenofemoral junction: treated as deep vein thrombosis with full-dose therapeutic anticoagulation for 3 months due to high risk of progression into the common femoral vein.
- Trousseau syndrome clinical significance: recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis is a paraneoplastic marker indicating underlying visceral adenocarcinoma (especially pancreatic cancer).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 54-year-old woman presenting with a painful, erythematous, palpable 8-cm cord over the medial lower calf with duplex ultrasound confirming great saphenous vein SVT ending 12 cm below the SFJ.
- A 62-year-old man presenting with acute groin tenderness whose duplex scan reveals great saphenous vein thrombosis extending to within 1.5 cm of the common femoral vein.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42147034**: *Catheter-Related Superficial Venous Thrombosis of the Upper Extremity: A Narrative Review of Current Evidence, Diagnostic Pathways, and Management Strategies.* (2026) [review] - Journal of blood medicine

## [1683] surgical site infection prevention

**Cluster**: surgical site infection prevention | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Surgical site infections (SSIs) represent the most frequent healthcare-associated infection among surgical patients, contributing to prolonged hospitalization, readmission, sepsis, and substantial mortality. Prevention requires meticulous adherence to an evidence-based perioperative care bundle encompassing preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative interventions. Core components include timely weight-adjusted prophylactic antibiotics administered within 60 minutes prior to incision, alcohol-based chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, normothermia maintenance, intraoperative oxygenation, and tight glycaemic control.

### Core Teaching Points
- Preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis must be completely infused within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision (120 minutes for vancomycin or fluoroquinolones) to achieve bactericidal tissue levels during incision, and re-dosed intraoperatively if procedure duration exceeds two half-lives of the antibiotic. (PMID 42616534)
- Preoperative hair removal, if necessary, must be performed immediately prior to surgery using electric clippers; routine manual razors with blades are strictly contraindicated as they cause microscopic skin abrasions that harbor bacteria and dramatically increase SSI rates. (PMID 42765564)
- Alcoholic chlorhexidine gluconate skin preparation is significantly superior to aqueous povidone-iodine in reducing surgical site infections in clean-contaminated and clean procedures. (PMID 42852549)
- Prophylactic antibiotic administration should NOT be continued postoperatively beyond wound closure for uncomplicated clean and clean-contaminated procedures; continuing antibiotics for 24-48 hours post-op provides zero SSI reduction while driving Clostridioides difficile colitis and antibiotic resistance. (PMID 41677813)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy and safety of intrawound vancomycin powder application in reducing deep periprosthetic and spinal surgical site infections.
- Value of routine closed-incision negative pressure wound therapy (ciNPWT) over conventional sterile dressings in high-risk abdominal wounds.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Optimal timing of preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis (within 60 minutes prior to incision) and intraoperative re-dosing intervals (e.g., cefazolin re-dosed at 4 hours).
- Hair removal techniques: electric clippers over razors to prevent microabrasions and SSI.
- Evidence-based cessation of prophylactic antibiotics at wound closure versus inappropriate routine 24-hour postoperative continuation.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 62-year-old obese diabetic male is scheduled for elective sigmoid resection for diverticular disease; the surgical trainee plans preoperative skin preparation and timing of prophylactic IV cefazolin plus metronidazole.
- Following an uncomplicated 2-hour total knee arthroplasty, the surgical resident writes an order for IV cefazolin every 8 hours for 3 days 'for infection prevention'.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

## [1684] Surgical site infection: prevention and management

**Cluster**: surgical site infection prevention and management | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Surgical site infections (SSIs) are the most common healthcare-associated infections among surgical patients, contributing to prolonged hospitalization, readmission, and morbidity. Implementing evidence-based preventive care bundles across preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative phases significantly reduces infection rates.

### Core Teaching Points
- CDC classifications divide SSIs into: (1) Superficial incisional (involves only skin and subcutaneous tissue within 30 days), (2) Deep incisional (involves deep soft tissues, fascial and muscle layers within 30 to 90 days), and (3) Organ/Space (involves any anatomical part opened or manipulated during surgery within 30 to 90 days). (PMID 42616534)
- Preoperative hair removal: routine shaving with razors causes microscopic skin abrasions that harbor bacteria and significantly increases SSI rates; if hair removal is necessary, electric clippers with a single-use blade immediately prior to surgery must be used. (PMID 42765564)
- Surgical skin antisepsis: chlorhexidine gluconate in an alcoholic solution (2% chlorhexidine in 70% isopropyl alcohol) is guideline-preferred (WHO, CDC, NICE) over povidone-iodine due to superior residual bactericidal persistence and lower SSI incidence in clean-contaminated surgeries. (PMID 42852549)
- Intraoperative physiological optimization requires: maintaining strict normothermia (core temperature >=36.0 C via active forced-air warming blankets, preventing hypothermia-induced vasoconstriction and impaired neutrophil killing), perioperative glycemic control (blood glucose <200 mg/dL / <11 mmol/L in all patients), and maintaining adequate tissue oxygenation via normovolemia. (PMID 42409269)
- Management of established incisional SSI requires: opening the surgical incision to evacuate purulent collections, debriding devitalized tissue, taking deep tissue specimens for Gram stain and culture, and packing with saline-moistened sterile gauze or applying negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT); systemic antibiotics are indicated only if systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia) or surrounding erythema >5 cm is present. (PMID 42601706)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical efficacy of prophylactic closed incisional negative pressure wound therapy (ciNPWT) in clean-contaminated high-risk abdominal incisions.
- Comparative effectiveness of supplemental high fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2 80% vs 30-35%) in reducing SSI rates in mechanically ventilated surgical patients.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Hair removal standard of care: hair should NOT be removed routinely; if required, electric clipping immediately before surgery is mandatory; razors are strictly contraindicated.
- Skin preparation agent of choice: alcoholic chlorhexidine gluconate is superior to aqueous povidone-iodine in preventing surgical site infections.
- Hypothermia prevention mechanism: maintaining core normothermia (>=36 C) prevents peripheral vasoconstriction and preserves neutrophil oxidative bactericidal burst.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 58-year-old woman on postoperative day 6 following an elective open sigmoid colectomy who develops low-grade fever, erythema, and purulent discharge from the midline wound.
- A surgical safety committee reviewing preoperative preparation protocols to transition from disposable razors to single-use surgical clippers.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

- **PMID 42765564**: *Intrawound vancomycin for prevention of surgical site infection: meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - BJS open

## [1685] Surgical site infections: classification, risk factors, prophylaxis timing, MRSA decolonisation

**Cluster**: surgical site infections classification risk factors prophylaxis timing mrsa decolonisation | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Antimicrobial surgical prophylaxis is a time-critical intervention designed to achieve bactericidal tissue concentrations at the precise moment of incision. Adherence to strict administration windows, redosing intervals, and targeted MRSA screening prevents SSI without fostering antimicrobial resistance.

### Core Teaching Points
- Timing of surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis: intravenous antibiotics must be completely infused within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision (or within 120 minutes for agents with long infusion times like vancomycin or fluoroquinolones) to guarantee peak tissue drug concentrations at the moment of initial skin incision. (PMID 42601706)
- Postoperative discontinuation: antimicrobial prophylaxis should be discontinued within 24 hours of surgery completion (or immediately at wound closure); continuing prophylactic antibiotics postoperatively does NOT reduce SSI rates and promotes Clostridioides difficile colitis and multidrug-resistant pathogen emergence. (PMID 42767272)
- Intraoperative redosing is mandatory if the procedure duration exceeds two half-lives of the antibiotic (e.g., redose cefazolin every 3 to 4 hours) or in cases of massive intraoperative blood loss (>1,500 mL) to maintain adequate minimum inhibitory concentrations. (PMID 42616534)
- Cefazolin (2 g IV for patients <120 kg, or 3 g IV for patients >=120 kg) is the standard workhorse prophylactic agent for clean and clean-contaminated procedures; broad-spectrum agents with anaerobic coverage (cefazolin plus metronidazole, or cefoxitin) are required for colorectal surgery. (PMID 42765564)
- Targeted preoperative MRSA screening and decolonization (nasal mupirocin 2% ointment twice daily for 5 days combined with daily 4% chlorhexidine body washes) prior to elective high-risk procedures (orthopedic arthroplasty and cardiac surgery) significantly reduces S. aureus surgical site infections; vancomycin is added to cefazolin only for confirmed MRSA carriers or high-risk institutional settings. (PMID 42852549)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Universal versus targeted preoperative nasal mupirocin decolonization in community hospitals with low baseline MRSA prevalence.
- Safety and allergy de-labeling protocols for utilizing cefazolin in patients with non-anaphylactic historical penicillin allergies.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Timing window for standard antibiotic prophylaxis: complete infusion within 60 minutes prior to surgical incision; vancomycin requires 120 minutes due to Red Man syndrome.
- Postoperative antibiotic duration rule: prophylactic antibiotics must be stopped within 24 hours post-op (or at wound closure); prolonged continuation is not guideline-adherent.
- Cefazolin weight-based dosing: 2 g for patients <120 kg; increased to 3 g for patients weighing >=120 kg (or BMI >35).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 45-year-old man undergoing elective total hip replacement whose anesthesia record indicates cefazolin was administered 15 minutes after surgical skin incision.
- A 70-year-old woman scheduled for elective coronary artery bypass grafting whose preoperative nasal swab is positive for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 42767272**: *Factors Associated With Surgical Site Infections in Adults Following a Replacement of Weight-Bearing Joints: A Systematic Review.* (2026) [systematic review] - International wound journal

## [1686] Suspected melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancer and urgent referral

**Cluster**: suspected melanoma non melanoma skin cancer and urgent referral | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Suspected melanoma needs urgent specialist assessment and complete excision biopsy. Dermoscopy improves accuracy, and Breslow thickness determines wide excision margins and sentinel node biopsy.

### Core Teaching Points
- Pigmented lesions with asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variegation, diameter of 6 mm or more or evolution (ABCDE), or an 'ugly duckling' lesion, warrant urgent suspected-cancer referral. (PMID 42001686)
- Diagnosis is by complete excision biopsy with a narrow (about 2 mm) margin; incisional or shave biopsy is avoided where possible because accurate Breslow thickness drives management. (PMID 42001686)
- Dermoscopy raises diagnostic accuracy; melanoma features include an atypical network, irregular globules, blue-white veil and regression structures. (PMID 31562236)
- Wide local excision margins depend on Breslow thickness: 1 cm for in situ to 1 mm tumours, and 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, with 2 cm (2 to 3 cm in UK guidance) for tumours thicker than 2 mm. (PMID 31562236)
- Sentinel lymph node biopsy is offered for tumours of about 0.8 mm or thicker, or thinner with ulceration. (PMID 42001686)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with suspected melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancer and urgent referral.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- ABCDE features.
- Biopsy method.
- Excision margins by Breslow thickness.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An adult patient presenting with acute or subacute manifestations of suspected melanoma, non-melanoma skin cancer and urgent referral requiring immediate diagnostic confirmation and therapy.
- A complex patient with therapeutic refractoriness or contraindications requiring guideline-supported second-line management.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1687] suspected pulmonary embolism diagnosis YEARS algorithm D-dimer CT pulmonary angiography

**Cluster**: suspected pulmonary embolism diagnosis years algorithm d dimer ct pulmonary angiography | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency requiring rapid, systematic diagnostic evaluation to confirm or exclude pulmonary vascular occlusion while avoiding unnecessary CT radiation and contrast-induced nephropathy. The YEARS algorithm streamlines diagnostic evaluation using three clinical criteria: clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), hemoptysis, and whether PE is the most likely diagnosis. Combined with clinical probability-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs, YEARS safely rules out PE without CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) in up to 50% of suspected presentations, and has been validated across special populations including pregnant patients.

### Core Teaching Points
- The YEARS algorithm consists of 3 clinical items: (1) clinical signs of DVT, (2) hemoptysis, and (3) PE most likely diagnosis; in patients with 0 YEARS criteria, a D-dimer threshold of <1000 ng/mL safely excludes PE without imaging. (PMID 42283136)
- In patients with >=1 YEARS criteria, the standard D-dimer threshold of <500 ng/mL (or age-adjusted cutoff: age x 10 in patients >50 years) is applied to rule out PE without CTPA. (PMID 42790624)
- The pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm safely excludes PE in pregnant women without CTPA using compression ultrasonography (CUS) and YEARS-adjusted D-dimer, avoiding fetal and maternal breast ionizing radiation. (PMID 36436972)
- When imaging is required, CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the definitive gold standard imaging modality, providing direct visualization of filling defects in pulmonary arterial branches down to subsegmental levels. (PMID 40200307)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Clinical significance and necessity of therapeutic anticoagulation for isolated subsegmental pulmonary embolism (SSPE) without concurrent DVT in low-risk patients.
- Diagnostic accuracy of ventilation-perfusion SPECT imaging versus low-dose CTPA in patients with severe renal impairment or severe contrast allergy.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Application of the YEARS diagnostic thresholds: explaining why patients with zero criteria use a 1000 ng/mL cutoff whereas those with >=1 use 500 ng/mL.
- Applying age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 ug/L for patients >50 years) in non-YEARS conventional algorithms to improve specificity in older adults.
- Initial workup of suspected PE in pregnancy: bilateral lower extremity compression duplex ultrasound prior to thoracic radiation.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 28-year-old woman taking oral contraceptives presents with mild pleuritic chest pain; she has no leg swelling, no hemoptysis, and muscular strain is deemed more likely (0 YEARS criteria); her D-dimer is 780 ng/mL.
- A 26-week pregnant female presents with sudden dyspnoea and right leg calf swelling; the clinical team initiates the pregnancy-adapted YEARS diagnostic pathway.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

### Evidence Sources

## [1688] Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine, temporary pacing, transcutaneous pacing

**Cluster**: symptomatic bradycardia atropine temporary pacing transcutaneous pacing | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Symptomatic bradycardia with adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure) is treated with atropine, then second-line drugs or pacing. Infranodal block often fails to respond to atropine.

### Core Teaching Points
- For unstable bradycardia, give atropine 500 mcg to 1 mg IV every 3 to 5 minutes up to 3 mg; it is often ineffective in infranodal (Mobitz II or complete) block, in heart transplant recipients and in some drug overdoses. (PMID 42001688)
- If atropine fails, options are transcutaneous pacing, adrenaline 2 to 10 mcg/min, or dopamine 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min while arranging transvenous pacing. (PMID 30462002)
- Transcutaneous pacing is painful and needs analgesia and sedation; it is a bridge. (PMID 30462002)
- Mobitz II, complete heart block with a wide QRS, or ventricular pauses of 3 seconds or more call for urgent transvenous pacing and planning for a permanent pacemaker. (PMID 30462002)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with symptomatic bradycardia: atropine, temporary pacing, transcutaneous pacing.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Adverse features that mandate treatment.
- Atropine dosing and limits.
- Second-line therapy.

### Case Generation Hooks
- An adult patient presenting with acute or subacute manifestations of symptomatic bradycardia: atropine, temporary pacing, transcutaneous pacing requiring immediate diagnostic confirmation and therapy.
- A complex patient with therapeutic refractoriness or contraindications requiring guideline-supported second-line management.

## [1689] syncope

**Cluster**: syncope | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery, caused by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. Syncope is categorized etiologically into reflex (neurally mediated: vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus hypersensitivity), orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure, volume depletion, drug-induced), and cardiac syncope (arrhythmic or structural). The initial clinical priority is identifying high-risk cardiac features—syncope during exertion, supine syncope, sudden palpitations preceding collapse, family history of premature sudden death, abnormal ECG, or known structural heart disease—which mandate urgent inpatient cardiac evaluation.

### Core Teaching Points
- Cardiac syncope (arrhythmic or structural heart disease) is the strongest independent predictor of sudden cardiac death and 1-year mortality, mandating immediate 12-lead ECG and urgent echocardiography whenever red flags are present. (PMID 29562304)
- A standard 12-lead ECG is mandatory in ALL patients presenting with syncope, screening for high-risk electrical abnormalities: prolonged or short QTc, Brugada pattern, pre-excitation (delta wave / WPW), bifascicular block, high-degree AV block, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (epsilon waves). (PMID 25980576)
- Vasovagal syncope (the most common cause in young, healthy individuals) is characterized by classic prodromal autonomic symptoms (lightheadedness, diaphoresis, pallor, nausea, warmth) triggered by prolonged standing, pain, emotional distress, or venepuncture. (PMID 21135810)
- Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed by a sustained drop in systolic BP >=20 mmHg and/or diastolic BP >=10 mmHg (or a fall in systolic to <90 mmHg) within 3 minutes of standing from a supine position, commonly exacerbated by polypharmacy (vasodilators, diuretics). (PMID 16505178)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Diagnostic yield and cost-effectiveness of early insertable cardiac monitors (implantable loop recorders [ILRs]) compared to conventional Holter monitoring in unexplained recurrent syncope.
- Efficacy of pacemaker implantation in older patients with recurrent refractory vasovagal syncope with documented cardioinhibitory asystole.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Differentiating high-risk cardiac syncope (exertional, supine, sudden collapse without prodrome) from benign vasovagal syncope.
- Recognizing high-risk ECG findings in unexplained syncope that warrant immediate admission and continuous telemetry monitoring.
- Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension and identifying causative pharmacological agents.

## [1690] Syncope and postural hypotension

**Cluster**: syncope and postural hypotension | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness (TLOC) caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion, characterized by rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery. Differentiating benign orthostatic and reflex syncope from cardiac syncope requires systematic orthostatic vital sign measurement and risk stratification.

### Core Teaching Points
- Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is defined as a sustained reduction in systolic blood pressure of >=20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of >=10 mmHg (or a fall in SBP to <90 mmHg) within 3 minutes of standing or head-up tilt to >=60 degrees. (PMID 25980576)
- Pathophysiological categories of orthostatic hypotension include: (1) Non-neurogenic (hypovolemia, dehydration, blood loss, vasodilating medications, diuretics, alcohol), and (2) Neurogenic (primary autonomic failure in Parkinson disease, Multiple System Atrophy, pure autonomic failure; or secondary autonomic neuropathy in diabetes, amyloidosis, autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy). (PMID 41767005)
- Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) is characterized by an inadequate compensatory heart rate increase upon standing (typically <10–15 bpm rise despite severe hypotension) and postprandial/supine hypertension; diagnosis can be supported by measuring supine and standing plasma norepinephrine (failure of norepinephrine to double on standing confirms defective sympathetic efferent release). (PMID 41980511)
- Non-pharmacological interventions are foundational: review and deprescribe culprit antihypertensive medications, liberalize dietary fluid (2–2.5 L/day) and sodium intake (6–10 g/day), apply waist-high compression stockings and abdominal binders, elevate head of the bed 10–15 degrees at night, and teach physical counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, squatting). (PMID 41364925)
- Pharmacological therapy for refractory neurogenic orthostatic hypotension includes: Midodrine (selective peripheral alpha-1 adrenergic agonist), Droxidopa (norepinephrine prodrug), and Fludrocortisone (synthetic mineralocorticoid promoting renal sodium retention and plasma volume expansion; monitor for supine hypertension and hypokalemia). (PMID 25980576)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative long-term clinical efficacy and supine hypertension safety of droxidopa versus midodrine in multiple system atrophy.
- Role of pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor augmenting autonomic ganglionic transmission) as monotherapy for orthostatic hypotension.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension: sustained fall in SBP >=20 mmHg or DBP >=10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
- Distinguishing neurogenic from non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: neurogenic OH features blunted compensatory tachycardia (<10-15 bpm increase) due to baroreflex failure.
- Fludrocortisone monitoring hazard: promotes volume expansion but exacerbates supine hypertension, predisposing to nocturnal stroke and congestive heart failure.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease who feels dizzy upon standing, with supine BP 155/85 mmHg (HR 72) falling to 95/55 mmHg (HR 76) at 2 minutes of standing.
- An 80-year-old woman taking hydrochlorothiazide and amlodipine presenting with recurrent syncopal falls upon getting out of bed in the morning.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1691] Syncope evaluation and pacing indications

**Cluster**: syncope evaluation and pacing indications | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Evaluation of syncope requires distinguishing benign reflex/orthostatic etiologies from life-threatening cardiogenic causes. Permanent pacemaker implantation is indicated for high-grade atrioventricular block, symptomatic sick sinus syndrome, and severe cardioinhibitory reflex syncope meeting strict diagnostic criteria.

### Core Teaching Points
- Diagnostic workup of syncope prioritizes distinguishing cardiac (arrhythmic or structural) causes from vasovagal and orthostatic syncope; persistent unexplained syncope in patients with underlying structural heart disease or abnormal baseline ECG carries high risk of sudden cardiac death. (PMID 40818650)
- Class I indications for permanent cardiac pacing in acquired atrioventricular (AV) block include complete third-degree AV block, advanced/high-grade second-degree AV block, and Mobitz Type II second-degree AV block, regardless of symptoms. (PMID 41783543)
- In sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction), pacing is indicated only when syncope or presyncope is directly documented to correlate with symptomatic sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or sinoatrial exit block. (PMID 21135810)
- For recurrent cardioinhibitory reflex syncope in patients aged >=40 years, dual-chamber pacemaker implantation is indicated when documentation of asystolic pauses >=3 seconds (with syncope) or >=6 seconds (asymptomatic) is confirmed during tilt-table testing or implantable loop recorder (ILR) monitoring. (PMID 40818650)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of closed-loop stimulation (CLS) pacing versus conventional dual-chamber DDD pacing in suppressing vasovagal syncope recurrence.
- Threshold for prophylactic pacemaker implantation in asymptomatic patients with alternating bundle branch block.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- ECG red flags in syncope: bifascicular block, Mobitz II second-degree AV block, prolonged QT interval, Brugada pattern, or pre-excitation (WPW).
- Pacing threshold in carotid sinus hypersensitivity: reproduction of syncope with asystole >3 seconds during carotid sinus massage confirms cardioinhibitory subtype.
- Mobitz I vs Mobitz II pacing indications: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) usually does not require pacing unless symptomatic; Mobitz II always warrants permanent pacing.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 74-year-old man presenting with sudden drop attacks without aura whose ECG demonstrates right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block (bifascicular block).
- A 45-year-old woman with recurrent traumatic syncopal episodes whose 3-month implantable loop recorder captures a 6.2-second sinus pause coincident with collapse.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

- **PMID 41783543**: *Empiric pacing in unexplained syncope and bifascicular block: A systematic review and meta-analysis.* (2026) [meta-analysis] - International journal of cardiology. Heart & vasculature

## [1692] Syncope evaluation: tilt table testing, loop recorder, reflex vs cardiac causes

**Cluster**: syncope evaluation tilt table testing loop recorder reflex vs cardiac causes | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Syncope evaluation starts with history, examination, orthostatic blood pressure and ECG to separate reflex, orthostatic and cardiac causes. Implantable loop recorders have the best yield for recurrent unexplained syncope.

### Core Teaching Points
- Features suggesting cardiac syncope include sudden onset without prodrome, onset during exertion or supine, abnormal ECG and structural heart disease; reflex syncope has triggers and prodrome. (PMID 42001692)
- Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed by a sustained systolic fall of 20 mmHg or diastolic 10 mmHg (or systolic below 90) within 3 minutes of standing. (PMID 29562364)
- Implantable loop recorders have a higher diagnostic yield than Holter monitoring or tilt testing for recurrent unexplained syncope of suspected arrhythmic origin. (PMID 29562364)
- Carotid sinus massage is considered in patients over 40 with unexplained syncope; a ventricular pause over 3 seconds or systolic fall of 50 mmHg or more indicates carotid sinus syndrome. (PMID 29562364)
- Tilt-table testing helps diagnose reflex syncope in selected cases. (PMID 42001692)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with syncope evaluation: tilt table testing, loop recorder, reflex vs cardiac causes.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Cardiac versus reflex clues.
- Orthostatic hypotension criteria.
- Role of the loop recorder.

## [1693] Synovial fluid analysis: WBC thresholds, crystals, viscosity, culture interpretation

**Cluster**: synovial fluid analysis wbc thresholds crystals viscosity culture interpretation | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Synovial fluid arthrocentesis and analysis is the definitive diagnostic procedure for acute arthritis. Evaluating fluid appearance, leukocyte count, differential, polarized microscopy for crystals, and microbiological culture allows reliable differentiation of non-inflammatory, inflammatory, and septic joint pathology.

### Core Teaching Points
- Synovial fluid classification divides effusions into four major categories: (1) Normal (clear, viscous, WBC <200/uL), (2) Non-inflammatory (clear/yellow, viscous, WBC 200–2,000/uL with <25% PMNs; osteoarthritis, trauma), (3) Inflammatory (cloudy/translucent, low viscosity, WBC 2,000–50,000/uL with >50% PMNs; RA, gout, pseudogout, spondyloarthritis), and (4) Septic (opaque/purulent, low viscosity, WBC >50,000/uL with >75–90% PMNs). (PMID 41211614)
- Viscosity is high in normal and non-inflammatory fluid (forming a 3–5 cm string between fingers / 'string sign' due to intact high-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid), and is low/watery in inflammatory and septic states where bacterial and leukocyte hyaluronidases depolymerize hyaluronic acid. (PMID 42233696)
- Compensated polarized light microscopy differentiates crystal types: Monosodium Urate (MSU / gout) crystals are needle-shaped with strongly negative birefringence (appearing bright yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis and blue when perpendicular); Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD / pseudogout) crystals are rhomboid/rod-shaped with weakly positive birefringence (appearing blue when aligned parallel and yellow when perpendicular). (PMID 42129958)
- Synovial fluid glucose is normally identical to serum glucose; in septic arthritis and severe rheumatoid arthritis, synovial glucose is markedly depressed (<50% of simultaneous blood glucose) due to leukocyte and bacterial consumption. (PMID 42519810)
- Microbiological culture: synovial fluid should be inoculated directly into blood culture bottles (aerobic and anaerobic) at the bedside, which significantly enhances bacterial recovery and yield compared to standard sterile specimen cups, particularly for fastidious organisms (Kingella kingae in children, Neisseria, and Streptococci). (PMID 41211614)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Diagnostic utility of automated synovial fluid PCR syndromic panels in patients with suspected septic arthritis who received empiric antibiotics prior to arthrocentesis.
- Significance of intracellular versus extracellular crystals in predicting true acute crystal-induced flare versus incidental background crystalluria.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Compensated polarized light microscopy rules: Gout (MSU) = needle-shaped, strongly negative birefringence, yellow when parallel; Pseudogout (CPPD) = rhomboid, weakly positive birefringence, blue when parallel.
- Synovial leukocyte cutoffs: Non-inflammatory = <2,000 WBC/uL; Inflammatory = 2,000–50,000 WBC/uL; Septic = >50,000 WBC/uL with >90% PMNs.
- Blood culture bottle inoculation: direct bedside inoculation of synovial fluid into blood culture media dramatically increases culture sensitivity in septic arthritis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 56-year-old man presenting with acute podagra of the first MTP joint whose aspirated fluid reveals intracellular needle-shaped crystals that turn yellow parallel to the slow axis.
- A 72-year-old woman with an acutely swollen right knee yielding cloudy yellow fluid with 38,000 WBC/uL and weakly positive rhomboid-shaped crystals.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1694] Syphilis: staging, serology interpretation, penicillin treatment, neurosyphilis management

**Cluster**: syphilis staging serology interpretation penicillin treatment neurosyphilis management | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Syphilis is staged clinically, confirmed with treponemal and non-treponemal serology, and treated with benzathine penicillin G for early and late latent disease, and intravenous benzylpenicillin for neurosyphilis.

### Core Teaching Points
- Primary syphilis presents with a painless indurated chancre; secondary with a non-itchy rash including palms and soles, condylomata lata and lymphadenopathy. (PMID 42001694)
- Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) is treated with a single dose of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM. (PMID 33956699)
- Late latent and tertiary syphilis (gummatous, cardiovascular) are treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks. (PMID 33956699)
- Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated with IV benzylpenicillin 18 to 24 million units daily for 10 to 14 days; lumbar puncture is performed when neurological, ocular or otic features are present. (PMID 33956699)
- Diagnosis uses a treponemal test (EIA/TPPA) with a non-treponemal titre (RPR/VDRL); treatment response is a fourfold titre fall, and the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may follow the first dose. (PMID 42001694)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal duration, dosing adjustments, and sequencing of therapy in high-risk or multimorbid patients presenting with syphilis: staging, serology interpretation, penicillin treatment, neurosyphilis management.
- Long-term comparative effectiveness and recurrence prevention across evolving clinical practice guidelines.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles

## [1695] Syringomyelia: Chiari malformation associations, shunt indications

**Cluster**: syringomyelia chiari malformation associations shunt indications | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Syringomyelia is a neurological disorder characterized by the development of a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord parenchyma. Most commonly associated with Chiari I malformation, it presents with a classic dissociated sensory loss and requires neurosurgical restoration of normal cerebrospinal fluid dynamics.

### Core Teaching Points
- Syringomyelia most frequently results from obstruction to normal pulsatile cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow at the foramen magnum; Chiari I malformation (downward herniation of cerebellar tonsils >5 mm below the foramen magnum) accounts for >50–70% of non-traumatic syringomyelia cases. (PMID 41381820)
- Secondary non-Chiari etiologies include spinal cord trauma (post-traumatic syringomyelia developing months to years after injury), spinal arachnoiditis (infectious, post-surgical), spinal cord tumors (ependymoma, hemangioblastoma), and tethered cord syndrome. (PMID 41111088)
- The classic clinical presentation is a 'dissociated sensory loss' in a cape-like distribution across the shoulders, arms, and upper torso: loss of pain and temperature sensation with complete preservation of light touch, vibration, and proprioception, caused by the expanding syrinx disrupting crossing second-order spinothalamic neurons in the anterior white commissure. (PMID 41796392)
- Progression of the syrinx into anterior horn gray matter causes lower motor neuron weakness, muscle atrophy, and fasciculations in the hands and arms, while compression of lateral corticospinal tracts produces spastic paraparesis and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities; extension into the brainstem is termed syringobulbia (producing vocal cord paralysis, dysphagia, and tongue wasting). (PMID 41317435)
- Surgical management: Posterior Fossa Decompression (PFD—suboccipital craniectomy, C1 laminectomy, and duraplasty) is the primary definitive surgery for Chiari I-associated syringomyelia, restoring normal CSF dynamics at the craniovertebral junction and leading to syrinx collapse in >80% of cases; direct syrinx shunting (syringosubarachnoid or syringoperitoneal shunt) is reserved for non-communicating post-traumatic or post-inflammatory syringes refractory to decompression. (PMID 40865295)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Management of asymptomatic, incidentally detected Chiari I malformations with small stable non-expansile syringes on cervical MRI.
- Failure rates and optimal revision strategies for arachnoid scarring following previous posterior fossa duraplasty.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Anatomical basis of dissociated sensory loss: selective destruction of decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, sparing dorsal columns (proprioception intact).
- First-line surgical treatment for Chiari-associated syrinx: posterior fossa suboccipital craniectomy and duraplasty (restoring CSF flow); direct syrinx shunts are avoided as initial therapy.
- Chiari I diagnostic MRI threshold: caudal herniation of one or both cerebellar tonsils >=5 mm below the level of the foramen magnum.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 32-year-old woman presenting with painless cigarette burns on her fingertips and hands, whose neurological exam confirms absent pinprick sensation in a cape-like distribution across both shoulders.
- A 40-year-old man with Chiari I malformation and a large holocord syrinx undergoing posterior fossa decompression with C1 laminectomy.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1696] systemic analgesia

**Cluster**: systemic analgesia | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Systemic analgesia forms the pharmacological backbone of acute and chronic pain management, integrating non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs), adjuvant agents (gabapentinoids, ketamine, alpha-2 agonists), and opioids. The World Health Organization (WHO) analgesic ladder and modern multimodal opioid-sparing protocols emphasize combining analgesics with distinct mechanisms of action to achieve synergistic pain relief while minimizing opioid-related adverse effects (hypoventilation, sedation, ileus, hyperalgesia, dependency). Safe administration requires tailoring drug selection and dosing to renal function, hepatic reserve, gastrointestinal bleeding risk, cardiovascular co-morbidities, and individual patient age.

### Core Teaching Points
- Multimodal systemic analgesia—combining paracetamol, NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors, and regional blocks—significantly reduces 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption and accelerates functional recovery compared to opioid monotherapy. (PMID 42153651)
- Intravenous non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., ketorolac) provide potent opioid-sparing analgesia, but are contraindicated in acute kidney injury, advanced CKD (eGFR <30), active gastrointestinal ulceration, active bleeding, and immediately prior to high-risk vascular or spinal surgeries. (PMID 42304663)
- Low-dose sub-dissociative ketamine infusions (0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg/h) provide potent NMDA receptor antagonism, reducing severe postoperative opioid tolerance, hyperalgesia, and chronic postsurgical pain syndromes without inducing psychomimetic side effects. (PMID 41860055)
- Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) with IV morphine, hydromorphone, or fentanyl provides superior patient satisfaction and analgesia over intermittent nurse-administered boluses; routine continuous basal infusions should be avoided in opioid-naive patients to prevent fatal nocturnal respiratory depression. (PMID 42585876)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Role and optimal duration of perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusions in non-abdominal surgical cohorts.
- Comparative long-term safety and persistent post-surgical pain prevention with perioperative gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) given recent concerns over respiratory depression.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Risks of routine basal rate infusions in intravenous opioid patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) in opioid-naive adults (increased risk of life-threatening respiratory depression).
- Mechanisms and indications of sub-dissociative ketamine infusions in managing acute severe pain and opioid-tolerant patients.
- Absolute contraindications to systemic NSAIDs in acute perioperative and critically ill clinical settings.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 48-year-old opioid-naive male post-laparotomy receives IV hydromorphone PCA; the surgical team considers whether adding a continuous overnight basal infusion is safe.
- A 35-year-old patient with severe acute pancreatitis experiences unremitting pain despite escalating IV fentanyl doses; sub-dissociative ketamine infusion is initiated.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1697] systemic lupus erythematosus

**Cluster**: systemic lupus erythematosus | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a prototypical systemic autoimmune disorder characterized by loss of self-tolerance, immune complex deposition, and multiorgan inflammation predominantly affecting women of childbearing age (9:1 female-to-male ratio). Clinical manifestations range from cutaneous lesions (malar rash, discoid lupus), non-erosive polyarthritis, and serositis, to life-threatening lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric lupus, and severe haematologic cytopenias. Treatment paradigms emphasize early hydroxychloroquine for all patients (improving survival and preventing flares), strict glucocorticoid tapering, and early integration of immunosuppressives and targeted biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab).

### Core Teaching Points
- Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for ALL patients with systemic lupus erythematosus unless contraindicated, dosed at <=5 mg/kg actual body weight daily to reduce mortality, prevent organ flares, and minimize retinal toxicity risks. (PMID 42842145)
- Antinuclear antibody (ANA) tested by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells possesses >98% sensitivity, serving as the essential entry criterion in the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria; a negative ANA strongly argues against idiopathic SLE. (PMID 42579193)
- Lupus nephritis (occurring in up to 50% of patients) requires prompt diagnostic renal biopsy for ISN/RPS histologic classification (Class I through VI); Class III (focal) and Class IV (diffuse proliferative) nephritis carry highest risk of end-stage renal disease and mandate intensive induction with mycophenolate mofetil or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids. (PMID 42696514)
- Targeted biologic therapies—belimumab (anti-BAFF/BLyS) and anifrolumab (anti-type I interferon receptor monoclonal antibody)—significantly reduce disease activity, enable corticosteroid tapering, and prevent systemic disease flares in active SLE. (PMID 42718833)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of upfront triple therapy (mycophenolate mofetil, calcineurin inhibitors [voclosporin], and belimumab) in severe proliferative lupus nephritis.
- Safety and feasibility of complete withdrawal of maintenance glucocorticoid therapy in patients achieving long-term serological and clinical remission.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Universal indication and safe weight-based dosing threshold for hydroxychloroquine (<=5 mg/kg actual body weight) and retinal screening protocols.
- Identifying high-risk lupus nephritis (Class III/IV) requiring aggressive immunosuppressive induction with mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide.
- Interpretation of ANA, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Smith autoantibodies (anti-dsDNA correlates with nephritis activity and complement consumption; anti-Sm is highly specific).

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 24-year-old woman presents with photosensitive malar rash, symmetric small-joint polyarthritis of the hands, hair loss, and pleuritic chest pain; ANA is positive at 1:1280 (homogeneous).
- A 30-year-old woman with known SLE presents with new-onset periorbital oedema, BP 155/95 mmHg, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 3.2 g/g, and active urine sediment showing dysmorphic RBCs.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1698] Systemic lupus erythematosus biologic therapy

**Cluster**: systemic lupus erythematosus biologic therapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Biologic therapies in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) provide targeted immunosuppression directed at pathogenic B-cell survival factors and type I interferon signaling pathways. Integrating approved biologics alongside conventional synthetic therapy enables corticosteroid minimization and durable clinical remission.

### Core Teaching Points
- Belimumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds and neutralizes soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS / BAFF)—was the first targeted biologic approved for active autoantibody-positive SLE; it inhibits B-cell survival and differentiation, significantly reducing SLE disease flares and corticosteroid requirements (BLISS trials). (PMID 42552165)
- In active lupus nephritis (LN), the landmark BLISS-LN trial demonstrated that adding belimumab to standard induction therapy (mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide) significantly improved primary efficacy renal response and reduced the risk of renal-related events or death. (PMID 42842145)
- Anifrolumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting the type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1)—blocks the downstream biological activity of all type I interferons (IFN-alpha, IFN-beta); the TULIP trials established that anifrolumab significantly improves composite skin and musculoskeletal disease activity in active moderate-to-severe SLE. (PMID 42579193)
- Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) is utilized off-label as evidence-based therapy for severe, refractory lupus manifestations: refractory Class III/IV lupus nephritis, severe immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), and central nervous system neuropsychiatric lupus. (PMID 42696514)
- Targeted biologic therapy allows substantial glucocorticoid minimization: international EULAR guidelines establish a clinical target of tapering maintenance prednisone to <=5 mg/day (or complete withdrawal) to prevent irreversible cumulative organ damage. (PMID 42718833)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Efficacy of dual B-cell targeted therapy (sequential rituximab followed by belimumab) in preventing compensatory BLyS surges and sustaining remission in severe lupus nephritis.
- Risk of herpes zoster reactivation during anifrolumab therapy and optimal timing for recombinant zoster vaccination (Shingrix).

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Belimumab molecular target: binds soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF) to inhibit autoreactive B-cell survival and autoantibody production.
- Anifrolumab mechanism of action: blocks type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1), dampening the pathogenic interferon gene signature in SLE.
- BLISS-LN trial clinical impact: adding belimumab to standard induction therapy improves complete renal response and slows renal function decline in lupus nephritis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 32-year-old woman with active SLE experiencing persistent polyarthritis, malar rash, and positive anti-dsDNA despite hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate, started on IV belimumab.
- A 28-year-old woman with refractory biopsy-proven Class IV lupus nephritis on mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone who receives add-on B-cell depletion with rituximab.

## [1699] Systemic Sclerosis

**Cluster**: systemic sclerosis | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is a multisystem autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by a triad of microvascular obliterative vasculopathy, systemic immune activation with autoantibody production, and widespread progressive tissue fibrosis of skin and internal organs.

### Core Teaching Points
- Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is broadly classified into two major cutaneous subsets: Limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc, formerly CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia; skin thickening restricted to hands, face, and distal elbows/knees) and Diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc: rapid skin thickening extending proximally to trunk and thighs, carrying high early visceral organ failure risk). (PMID 42391056)
- Autoantibody profiles strongly correlate with clinical phenotypes: Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are classic for lcSSc (associated with severe Raynaud's, digital ulcers, and late development of isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension [PAH]); Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) is characteristic of dcSSc (strongly associated with progressive pulmonary fibrosis / SSc-ILD); Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are linked to rapidly progressive diffuse skin disease and a high risk of scleroderma renal crisis. (PMID 42599596)
- Raynaud phenomenon is the universal early presenting sign (>95% of patients); nailfold capillaroscopy is an essential diagnostic tool revealing early microvascular architectural changes: dilated giant capillary loops, microhemorrhages, and progressive capillary loss/avascular areas. (PMID 42322931)
- Leading causes of mortality in modern systemic sclerosis are pulmonary complications: Interstitial Lung Disease (SSc-ILD, developing in up to 80% of dcSSc) and Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH, developing in 10–15% of lcSSc); baseline high-resolution CT of the chest, pulmonary function tests with DLCO, and annual screening echocardiography are mandatory. (PMID 42780375)
- Targeted organ-specific pharmacotherapy: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) for Raynaud's and digital ulcers; mycophenolate mofetil or nintedanib for active SSc-ILD; oral captopril for scleroderma renal crisis; and ERA/PDE-5i combinations for pulmonary arterial hypertension. (PMID 42048834)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Therapeutic role and patient selection criteria for autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in severe, rapidly progressive diffuse systemic sclerosis.
- Clinical utility of novel antifibrotic and anti-IL-6 combinations in slowing multi-organ dermal and pulmonary fibrosis.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Antibody-phenotype correlations: Anti-Scl-70 predicts interstitial lung disease; anti-centromere predicts late pulmonary arterial hypertension; anti-RNA polymerase III predicts scleroderma renal crisis.
- Leading causes of death: pulmonary involvement (SSc-ILD and PAH) has surpassed renal crisis as the primary cause of scleroderma mortality.
- Diagnostic utility of nailfold capillaroscopy: detects giant enlarged capillary loops and avascular drop-out areas, distinguishing primary Raynaud from secondary autoimmune systemic sclerosis.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 42-year-old woman presenting with severe cold-induced digital triphasic color changes, sclerodactyly of both hands, facial telangiectasias, and positive anti-centromere antibodies.
- A 38-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma and anti-Scl-70 antibodies presenting with progressive exertional dyspnea and bibasilar crackles, whose HRCT shows non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP).

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1700] Systemic sclerosis interstitial lung disease

**Cluster**: systemic sclerosis interstitial lung disease | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD) is the leading cause of mortality in systemic sclerosis, affecting up to 80% of patients on imaging. Early screening with high-resolution chest CT and pulmonary function tests guides timely combination immunosuppression and antifibrotic therapy.

### Core Teaching Points
- Interstitial lung disease (ILD) occurs in both diffuse and limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, with the highest prevalence and most rapid progression occurring in patients with dcSSc, male sex, older age, and anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) autoantibodies. (PMID 41810839)
- High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest is mandatory at baseline for all patients with systemic sclerosis; the predominant radiological and histological pattern in SSc-ILD is Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP, present in 70–80%), characterized by bilateral, symmetric, basilar ground-glass opacities with traction bronchiectasis and relative subpleural sparing; UIP pattern occurs in 15–20%. (PMID 40685839)
- The Scleroderma Lung Study I and II (SLS I and II) established Mycophenolate Mofetil (MMF, target 2 to 3 g daily) as the preferred first-line immunosuppressive agent for active SSc-ILD, demonstrating equivalent stabilization of forced vital capacity (FVC) with vastly superior safety and tolerability compared to oral cyclophosphamide. (PMID 40197088)
- In patients with progressive fibrosing SSc-ILD, the landmark SENSCIS trial demonstrated that adding the antifibrotic tyrosine kinase inhibitor nintedanib (150 mg twice daily) to baseline therapy significantly reduced the annual rate of decline in FVC by 44% (annual decline of -52.4 mL/year with nintedanib vs -93.3 mL/year with placebo, P=0.04). (PMID 37923862)
- The anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab (focuSSced trial) demonstrated preservation of lung function in patients with early diffuse cutaneous SSc with elevated inflammatory markers, earning regulatory approval for slowing FVC decline in SSc-ILD. (PMID 36559035)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Optimal threshold for combining upfront immunosuppression (MMF) with antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) versus sequential add-on upon documented FVC progression.
- Role of cyclophosphamide rescue followed by autologous stem cell transplantation in rapidly progressive SSc-ILD refractory to MMF.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Predominant HRCT pattern in SSc-ILD: Non-Specific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP) with bilateral basal ground-glass opacities and subpleural sparing, contrasting with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP).
- First-line immunosuppressive of choice: mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the preferred standard first-line agent based on the Scleroderma Lung Study II.
- SENSCIS trial landmark outcome: nintedanib (antifibrotic TKI) significantly reduces the annual rate of FVC decline in systemic sclerosis-associated ILD.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 46-year-old woman with newly diagnosed diffuse systemic sclerosis and anti-Scl-70 antibodies whose baseline HRCT demonstrates bibasilar ground-glass opacities with an FVC of 72% predicted.
- A 52-year-old woman with SSc-ILD on maintenance mycophenolate mofetil who exhibits a 6% decline in FVC over 12 months, evaluated for combination therapy with nintedanib.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.

## [1702] takayasu arteritis biologic therapy

**Cluster**: takayasu arteritis biologic therapy | **Status**: published

### Clinical Mentor Synopsis
Takayasu arteritis (TAK) is a rare, chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting the aorta, its primary branches, and the pulmonary arteries, most commonly presenting in young females under 40 years of age. Inflammatory panarteritis leads to wall thickening, luminal stenosis, occlusion, and aneurysm formation, manifesting clinically as absent peripheral pulses, vascular bruits, limb claudication, and severe renovascular hypertension. While high-dose corticosteroids achieve initial remission, over 50% of patients relapse upon steroid tapering; biologic therapies—particularly TNF inhibitors and IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab)—serve as essential steroid-sparing agents for refractory or relapsing disease.

### Core Teaching Points
- First-line induction therapy for active Takayasu arteritis utilizes high-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day); however, early addition of a steroid-sparing disease-modifying agent is mandatory due to high relapse rates during steroid taper. (PMID 41345710)
- Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) and the anti-IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab demonstrate substantial efficacy in inducing clinical remission, halting angiographic disease progression, and permitting major corticosteroid dose reduction in refractory Takayasu arteritis. (PMID 42283880)
- Assessment of vascular disease activity requires specialized non-invasive vascular imaging (contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance angiography [MRA], CT angiography, or 18F-FDG PET/CT), as acute phase reactants (ESR, CRP) can be completely normal in up to 30-40% of patients with histologically active vascular inflammation. (PMID 40531440)
- Revascularization procedures (percutaneous angioplasty, stenting, or bypass surgery) must strictly be avoided during active vessel inflammation, as operating on inflamed vessels carries catastrophic risks of thrombosis, anastomotic disruption, and restenosis; procedures must be delayed until medical remission is achieved. (PMID 41860699)

### Key Controversies & Uncertainties
- Comparative long-term efficacy and vascular wall remodeling between anti-TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab in paediatric-onset Takayasu arteritis.
- Role of Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib) in patients failing both TNF and IL-6 targeted biologic agents.

### High-Yield MCQ Angles
- Selection of biologic therapies (anti-TNF agents vs tocilizumab) in steroid-refractory Takayasu arteritis.
- Timing of surgical or catheter-based vascular interventions: absolute requirement to induce stable immunosuppressive remission prior to elective revascularization.
- Limitations of acute phase reactants (ESR/CRP) in monitoring disease activity, highlighting the necessity of serial MRA or FDG-PET imaging.

### Case Generation Hooks
- A 23-year-old female presents with bilateral arm claudication, dizziness on standing, blood pressure unobtainable in the left arm (138/82 mmHg in right arm), and a loud carotid bruit; MRA reveals smooth narrowing of the aortic arch branches.
- A 28-year-old woman with active Takayasu arteritis relapses with progressive subclavian artery stenosis every time prednisone is tapered below 20 mg daily; the rheumatologist initiates biologic therapy with tocilizumab.

**Reviewer Gap**: Reviewers should confirm alignment with current local antimicrobial/formulary guidelines and relevant special population considerations.
